en:
...
A month ago, I received your letter. You wrote that Qiongqi Artificers had taken up residence in these mountains, and feared that some misfortune might befall me. It pains me to think that this worry has weighed on you so heavily that you have fallen ill and can neither eat nor drink at ease. My life is of little worth. It is not worth such anguish. You bear the burden of our household, so I beg you above all to take care of your health.
As for Qiongqi Artificers, there has never been cause for enmity between us. On the contrary, we have received kindness at their hands. The neighbors here all live in peace, so I ask that you do not trouble yourself needlessly.
And as for your urging me to come down from the mountain, I beg you to say no more of it. My wife and I have already been parted across two lifetimes. Please don't tear us apart again.

【坊记第三十】

子言之：“君子之道，辟则坊与，坊民之所不足者也。”大为之坊，民犹逾之。故君子礼以坊德，刑以坊淫，命以坊欲。
子云：“小人贫斯约，富斯骄；约斯盗，骄斯乱。”礼者，因人之情而为之节文，以为民坊者也。故圣人之制富贵也使民富不足以骄，贫不至于约，贵不慊于上，故乱益亡。子云：“贫而好乐，富而好礼，众而以宁者，天下其几矣。《诗》云：‘民之贪乱，宁为荼毒。』”故制：国不过千乘，都城不过百雉，家富不过百乘。以此坊民，诸侯犹有畔者。
子云：“夫礼者，所以章疑别微，以为民坊者也。”故贵贱有等，衣服有别，朝廷有位，则民有所让。子云：“天无二日，土无二王，家无二主，尊无二上，示民有君臣之别也。”《春秋》不称楚越之王丧，礼君不称天，大夫不称君，恐民之惑也。《诗》云：“相彼盍旦，尚犹患之。”子云：“君不与同姓同车，与异姓同车不同服，示民不嫌也。”以此坊民，民犹得同姓以弒其君。
子云：“君子辞贵不辞贱，辞富不辞贫，则乱益亡。”故君子与其使食浮于人也，宁使人浮于食。子云：“觞酒豆肉让而受恶，民犹犯齿；衽席之上让而坐下，民犹犯贵；朝廷之位让而就贱，民犹犯君。”《诗》云：“民之无良，相怨一方；受爵不让，至于已斯亡。”子云：“君子贵人而贱己，先人而后己，则民作让。”故称人之君曰君，自称其君曰寡君。子云：“利禄，先死者而后生者，则民不偝；先亡者而后存者，则民可以托。”《诗》云：“先君之思，以畜寡人。”以此坊民，民犹偝死而号无告。
子云：“有国家者，贵人而贱禄，则民兴让；尚技而贱车，则民兴艺。”故君子约言，小人先言。
……
en:
【Book of Records, Chapter 30: The Model of the Way】

The Master said: "The way of the gentleman is like a dike, guarding against the people's shortcomings." Even with great dikes, the people still cross them. Therefore, the gentleman uses rites to guard virtue, punishments to guard against excess, and mandates to guard against desire.
The Master said: "When the petty man is poor, he becomes restless; when rich, he becomes arrogant; restlessness leads to theft, and arrogance leads to disorder." Rites are the means by which human feelings are moderated and given form, serving as a dike for the people. Thus, the sage's regulation of wealth and honor ensures that the rich do not become arrogant, the poor do not fall into desperation, and the noble do not resent their superiors, so disorder gradually diminishes. The Master said: "Those who are poor yet love joy, rich yet love rites, and numerous yet remain peaceful—how few are such in the world! The Book of Songs says: 'The people, greedy for chaos, would rather suffer harm.'" Therefore, the regulations were set: a state should not exceed a thousand chariots, a capital city should not exceed a hundred zhi in circumference, and a noble family should not possess more than a hundred chariots. With these dikes for the people, even so, feudal lords still rebelled.
The Master said: "Rites are meant to clarify doubts and distinguish the subtle, serving as a dike for the people." Thus, there are ranks for noble and base, distinctions in clothing, and positions in the court, so that the people may yield to one another. The Master said: "There are not two suns in the sky, nor two kings on earth, nor two masters in a household, nor two supreme authorities—this shows the people the distinction between ruler and subject." The Spring and Autumn Annals does not refer to the funerals of the kings of Chu and Yue as such, rites do not call a ruler 'Heaven,' nor a high official 'ruler,' for fear of confusing the people. The Book of Songs says: 'Look at that bird calling before dawn; even it is resented.' The Master said: "A ruler does not ride in the same carriage with those of the same surname; with those of different surnames, he rides together but does not wear the same clothes, showing the people there is no ambiguity." With these dikes for the people, still the people managed to assassinate their rulers of the same surname.
The Master said: "The gentleman declines honor but not humility, declines wealth but not poverty, and thus disorder gradually diminishes." Therefore, the gentleman would rather let his virtue exceed his position than his position exceed his virtue. The Master said: "When offering a cup of wine and a dish of meat, yielding and accepting the inferior portion, the people still offend against age; when on mats and cushions, yielding and taking the lower seat, the people still offend against rank; when in court positions, yielding and taking the humble post, the people still offend against the ruler." The Book of Songs says: 'The people, lacking goodness, blame one another from their corners; receiving offices without yielding, until they themselves perish.' The Master said: "The gentleman honors others and humbles himself, puts others first and himself last, and thus the people rise to yielding." Therefore, one refers to another's ruler as 'ruler,' and to one's own ruler as 'my humble ruler.' The Master said: "When benefits and emoluments are given first to the dead and then to the living, the people will not turn their backs; when given first to the departed and then to the surviving, the people can be entrusted." The Book of Songs says: 'Thinking of the former ruler, to sustain me.' With these dikes for the people, still the people turned their backs on the dead and cried out without redress.
The Master said: "Those who hold states and families, honoring the worthy and devaluing emoluments, then the people will rise to yielding; esteeming skills and devaluing carriages, then the people will rise to arts." Therefore, the gentleman speaks little, while the petty man speaks first.
……

zh:
那是一个月黑风高之夜。
——此处本应该如此起笔。但史馆当值，向来有午时才到申时就走的优良传统，笔者也不能在此妄言污蔑本馆。
故而，事情发生之时，实则是一个日头不错的午后。
春和景明，正宜休憩。馆内众人各寻佳处安眠，唯有鸟雀叫声时时穿响在庭院之中。
突然！笔者在廊下惊醒，观日头尚未偏西，庭院鸟声皆静。
风过。笔者闻听一人惊呼：“这功夫！你是文津——”
竹叶簌簌。笔者听见另一道声音朗然笑道：“离馆之人，已不是江湖子弟，不敢称师门之名。”
先前一人怒道：“那你管什么江湖事！”
后一人笑道：“谁让江湖正撞上我呢。”
竹帘微动，半晌无声。
笔者在心中数到二十，才敢挑帘偷觑。
乍一看，未见人影。再定睛，方看清是那人身上的青袍与竹林同色，险险看不分明。
青袍。应是……馆中同僚？
簌啦啦——
笔者撩起的竹帘无端自落。再挑帘，人已经不见，唯有清风、绿竹而已。
en:
It was a dark, blustery night. That is how this account ought to begin.



But the Imperial Archives has a proud tradition: the day shift shows up at noon and clocks out by Shen hour. I would not dare smear my own institution with such baseless slander. So, truth be told, it happened on a perfectly pleasant afternoon.



The spring weather was mild, ideal for a nap. Everyone found a good spot to doze off. Only the birds kept calling in the courtyard now and then.



Then, all at once, I jolted awake in the covered walkway. The sun was still high, not yet sliding west, and the courtyard had gone dead quiet.



A gust passed.



I heard someone shout, "That technique! You are of the Inkbound..."



Bamboo leaves whispered. Another voice answered with a bright laugh. "I have left the hall. I am no longer one of you. I cannot go around borrowing my old master’s name."



The first voice snapped, "Then why stick your nose into jianghu business?"



The other laughed again. "Because jianghu walked straight into me."



The bamboo blind trembled. Then came a long stretch of silence.



I counted to twenty before I dared lift the blind and steal a look.



At first, there was no one. Then my eyes caught him. His blue-green robe was nearly the same shade as the bamboo, so close it was hard to make out at all.



A green robe. That meant... someone from the Archives?



Rustle.



The blind I had lifted dropped on its own. I raised it again, and he was gone.



There was nothing left but a cool breeze and the bamboo.

zh:
此乐谱在国内亡佚，唯诸古籍中留有名录逸闻。据《旧唐书·音乐志》、《太平广记·卷二〇三》等记载，秦王李世民平叛将刘武周之乱，河东士庶歌舞于道﹐军人利用军中旧曲填唱新词，欢庆胜利，遂有“秦王破阵”之曲流传于世，后编入乐府。贞观初年，唐太宗诏魏徵等人增撰歌词，吕才协律度曲，订为《秦王破阵乐》。
该曲在日本保留的唐乐古谱中有多个版本，版本之间各有差异，今取时间最早的《五弦谱》为参考。一般认为，《五弦谱》为日本人过录我国唐乐之谱，基本保留了唐乐原貌，现藏于日本东京都阳明文库。
en:
This musical score was lost in China but survives by name and anecdote in ancient texts. According to the Old Book of Tang: Treatise on Music and Extensive Records of the Taiping Era, the piece originated after Emperor Taizong defeated the rebel warlord Liu Wuzhou. The people of Hedong celebrated in the streets with song and dance. Soldiers adapted older military tunes with new lyrics to commemorate the victory, and thus the piece "The King of Qin Crushes the Enemies" was born, later entered the repertoire of the imperial music bureau. In the early Zhenguan era, Emperor Taizong ordered Wei Zheng and others to revise the lyrics, while Lu Cai arranged the melodies and harmonized the composition. The finalized work became known as Prince of Qin's Triumph. 
Several variants of the song survive in ancient Japanese Tang-music collections. Among them, the earliest version appears in the Five-String Score, believed to be a Japanese transcription of original Tang court music. This version, regarded as closest to the original, is currently preserved in the Yōmei Bunko in Tokyo.
Xie Changgeng

zh:
【梁惠王章句下】

庄暴见孟子，曰：暴见于王，王语暴以好乐，暴未有以对也。曰：好乐何如？
孟子曰：王之好乐甚，则齐国其庶几乎？
他日，见于王，曰：王尝语庄子以好乐，有诸？
王变乎色，曰：寡人非能好先王之乐也，直好世俗之乐耳。
曰：王之好乐甚，则齐其庶几乎？今之乐犹古之乐也。曰：可得闻与？
曰：独乐乐，与人乐乐，孰乐？曰：不若与人。
曰：与少乐乐，与众乐乐，孰乐？曰：不若与众。
臣请为王言乐。
今王鼓乐于此，百姓闻王钟鼓之声、管籥之音，举疾首蹙頞而相告曰：吾王之好鼓乐，夫何使我至于此极也？父子不相见，兄弟妻子离散。
今王田猎于此，百姓闻王车马之音，见羽旄之美，举疾首蹙頞而相告曰：吾王之好田猎，夫何使我至于此极也？父子不相见，兄弟妻子离散，此无他，不与民同乐也。
今王鼓乐于此，百姓闻王钟鼓之声、管籥之音，举欣欣然有喜色而相告曰：吾王庶几无疾病与？何以能鼓乐也？
今王田猎于此，百姓闻王车马之音，见羽旄之美，举欣欣然有喜色，而相告曰：吾王庶几无疾病与？何以能田猎也？此无他，与民同乐也。今王与百姓同乐，则王矣。
齐宣王问曰：文王之囿方七十里，有诸？
孟子对曰：于传有之。曰：若是其大乎？曰：民犹以为小也。
曰：寡人之囿方四十里，民犹以为大，何也？
曰：文王之囿方七十里，刍荛者往焉，雉兔者往焉，与民同之，民以为小，不亦宜乎？臣始至于境，问国之大禁，然后敢入。臣闻郊关之内，有囿方四十里，杀其麋鹿者如杀人之罪，则是方四十里为阱于国中，民以为大，不亦宜乎？
齐宣王问曰：交邻国有道乎？
孟子对曰：有。惟仁者为能以大事小，是故汤事葛，文王事混夷。惟智者为能以小事大，故大王事獯鬻，句践事吴。以大事小者，乐天者也；以小事大者，畏天者也。乐天者保天下，畏天者保其国。诗云：畏天之威，于时保之。
王曰：大哉言矣！寡人有疾，寡人好勇。
对曰：王请无好小勇。夫抚剑疾视曰：彼恶敢当我哉！此匹夫之勇，敌一人者也。王请大之。
诗云：王赫斯怒，爰整其旅，以遏徂莒，以笃周祜，以对于天下。此文王之勇也。文王一怒而安天下之民。
书曰：天降下民，作之君，作之师。惟曰其助上帝，宠之四方，有罪无罪，惟我在，天下曷敢有越厥志？一人衡行于天下，武王耻之。此武王之勇也。而武王亦一怒而安天下之民。今王亦一怒而安天下之民，民惟恐王之不好勇也。
齐宣王见孟子于雪宫，王曰：贤者亦有此乐乎？
孟子对曰：有。人不得，则非其上矣。不得而非其上者，非也；为民上而不与民同乐者，亦非也。乐民之乐者，民亦乐其乐；忧民之忧者，民亦忧其忧。乐以天下，忧以天下，然而不王者，未之有也。
昔者齐景公问于晏子曰：吾欲观于转附、朝舞，遵海而南，放于琅邪，吾何修而可以比于先王观也？
晏子对曰：善哉问也。天子适诸侯曰巡狩。巡狩者，巡所守也。诸侯朝于天子，曰述职。述职者，述所职也。无非事者。春省耕而补不足，秋省敛而助不给。夏谚曰：吾王不游，吾何以休？吾王不豫，吾何以助？一游一豫，为诸侯度。今也不然，师行而粮食，饥者弗食，劳者弗息，睊睊胥谗，民乃作慝。方命虐民，饮食若流，流连荒亡，为诸侯忧。从流下而忘反谓之流，从流上而忘反谓之连，从兽无厌谓之荒，乐酒无厌谓之亡。先王无流连之乐，荒亡之行，惟君所行也。
景公说，大戒于国，出舍于郊，于是始兴发，补不足，召大师曰：为我作君臣相说之乐。盖征招、角招是也。其诗曰：畜君何尤？畜君者，好君也。
齐宣王问曰：人皆谓我毁明堂，毁诸？已乎？
孟子对曰：夫明堂者，王者之堂也。王欲行王政，则勿毁之矣。
王曰：王政可得闻与？
对曰：昔者文王之治岐也，耕者九一，仕者世禄，关市讥而不征，泽梁无禁，罪人不孥，老而无妻曰鳏，老而无夫曰寡，老而无子曰独，幼而无父曰孤。此四者，天下之穷民而无告者。文王发政施仁，必先斯四者。诗云：哿矣富人，哀此茕独。王曰：善哉言乎！
曰：王如善之，则何为不行？
王曰：寡人有疾，寡人好货。
对曰：昔者公刘好货，诗云：乃积乃仓，乃裹糇粮。于橐于囊，思戢用光。弓矢斯张，干戈戚扬，爰方启行。故居者有积仓，行者有裹囊也，然后可以爰方启行。王如好货，与百姓同之，于王何有？
王曰：寡人有疾，寡人好色。
对曰：昔者大王好色，爱厥妃。诗云：古公亶甫，来朝走马。率西水浒，至于岐下。爰及姜女，聿来胥宇。当是诗也，内无怨女，外无旷夫。王如好色，与百姓同之，于王何有？
孟子谓齐宣王曰：王之臣有托其妻子于其友而之楚游者，比其反也，则冻馁其妻子，则如之何？王曰：弃之。
曰：士师不能治士，则如之何？王曰：已之。
曰：四境之内不治，则如之何？王顾左右而言他。
孟子见齐宣王曰：所谓故国者，非谓有乔木之谓也，有世臣之谓也。王无亲臣矣，昔者所进，今日不知其亡也。
王曰：吾何以识其不才而舍之？
曰：国君进贤，如不得己，将使卑逾尊，疏逾戚，可不慎与？左右皆曰贤，未可也；诸大夫皆曰贤，未可也；国人皆曰贤，然后察之；见贤焉，然后用之。左右皆曰不可，勿听；诸大夫皆曰不可，勿听；国人皆曰不可，然后察之；见不可焉，然后去之。左右皆曰可杀，勿听；诸大夫皆曰可杀，勿听；国人皆曰可杀，然后察之；见可杀焉，然后杀之，故曰国人杀之也。如此，然后可以为民父母。
齐宣王问曰：汤放桀，武王伐纣，有诸？
孟子对曰：于传有之。曰：臣弑其君，可乎？
曰：贼仁者谓之贼，贼义者谓之残，残贼之人，谓之一夫。闻诛一夫纣矣，未闻弑君也。
孟子谓齐宣王曰：为巨室，则必使工师求大木。工师得大木，则王喜，以为能胜其任也。匠人斫而小之，则王怒，以为不胜其任矣。夫人幼而学之，壮而欲行之，王曰：姑舍女所学而从我，则何如？今有璞玉于此，虽万镒，必使玉人雕琢之。至于治国家，则曰：姑舍女所学而从我，则何以异于教玉人雕琢玉哉？
齐人伐燕，胜之。宣王问曰：或谓寡人勿取，或谓寡人取之。以万乘之国伐万乘之国，五旬而举之，人力不至于此。不取必有天殃。取之何如？
孟子对曰：取之而燕民悦，则取之，古之人有行之者，武王是也。取之而燕民不悦，则勿取，古之人有行之者，文王是也。以万乘之国伐万乘之国，箪食壶浆以迎王师，岂有他哉？避水火也。如水益深，如火益热，亦运而已矣。
齐人伐燕，取之。诸侯将谋救燕，宣王曰：诸侯多谋伐寡人者，何以待之？
孟子对曰：臣闻七十里为政于天下者，汤是也。未闻以千里畏人者也。书曰：汤一征，自葛始。天下信之。东面而征，西夷怨，南面而征，北狄怨。曰：奚为后我？民望之若大旱之望云霓也，归市者不止，耕者不变。诛其君而吊其民，若时雨降，民大悦。书曰：徯我后，后来其苏。今燕虐其民，王往而征之，民以为将拯己于水火之中也，箪食壶浆以迎王师。若杀其父兄，系累其子弟，毁其宗庙，迁其重器，如之何其可也？天下固畏齐之强也，今又倍地而不行仁政，是动天下之兵也。王速出令，反其旄倪，止其重器，谋于燕众，置君而后去之，则犹可及止也。
邹与鲁𬮢，穆公问曰：吾有司死者三十三人，而民莫之死也。诛之，则不可胜诛；不诛，则疾视其长上之死而不救，如之何则可也？
孟子对曰：凶年饥岁，君之民老弱转乎沟壑，壮者散而之四方者，几千人矣。而君之仓廪实，府库充，有司莫以告，是上慢而残下也。曾子曰：戒之，戒之！出乎尔者，反乎尔者也。夫民今而后得反之也，君无尤焉。君行仁政，斯民亲其上，死其长矣。
en:
【King Hui of Liang, Part II】

Zhuang Bao went to see Mencius and said, "I had an audience with the king, and he told me of his love for music. I had no answer for him." Then he asked, "What is the significance of loving music?"
Mencius replied, "If the king's love for music is great, then the state of Qi is close to being well-governed, is it not?"
Another day, Mencius had an audience with the king and said, "Your Majesty once told Zhuang Bao of your love for music. Is this true?"
The king’s countenance changed, and he said, "I am not capable of appreciating the music of the ancient kings; I merely enjoy the popular music of today."
Mencius said, "If the king's love for music is great, then Qi is close to being well-governed. The music of today is no different from the music of antiquity." The king asked, "May I hear more about this?"
Mencius asked, "Which is more enjoyable: enjoying music alone, or enjoying it with others?" The king replied, "It is not as enjoyable as sharing it with others."
Mencius asked, "Which is more enjoyable: enjoying music with a few, or with many?" The king replied, "It is not as enjoyable as sharing it with many."
Mencius said, "Allow me to speak to Your Majesty about music."
"Suppose Your Majesty were to perform music here. If the people heard the sound of your bells, drums, pipes, and flutes, and all frowned with distress, saying to one another, 'Our king's love for music—why does it bring us to such an extreme? Fathers and sons cannot see each other, brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated.'"
"Suppose Your Majesty were to hunt here. If the people heard the sound of your carriages and horses, saw the beauty of your banners and plumes, and all frowned with distress, saying to one another, 'Our king's love for hunting—why does it bring us to such an extreme? Fathers and sons cannot see each other, brothers, wives, and children are scattered and separated.' This is for no other reason than that you do not share your joy with the people."
"Suppose Your Majesty were to perform music here. If the people heard the sound of your bells, drums, pipes, and flutes, and all beamed with joy, saying to one another, 'Our king must be free from illness—how else could he perform music?'"
"Suppose Your Majesty were to hunt here. If the people heard the sound of your carriages and horses, saw the beauty of your banners and plumes, and all beamed with joy, saying to one another, 'Our king must be free from illness—how else could he hunt?' This is for no other reason than that you share your joy with the people. If Your Majesty shares joy with the people, you will become a true king."
King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is it true that King Wen's hunting park was seventy li square?"
Mencius replied, "It is recorded as such." The king asked, "Was it really that large?" Mencius said, "The people still considered it small."
The king said, "My hunting park is forty li square, yet the people consider it large. Why is that?"
Mencius said, "King Wen's park was seventy li square, but grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers went there, and hunters of pheasants and hares went there. He shared it with the people, so they considered it small—is that not fitting? When I first arrived at your borders, I inquired about the great prohibitions of the state before daring to enter. I heard that within the suburbs, there is a park forty li square, and anyone who kills a deer in it is punished as if they had killed a person. Thus, these forty li are like a trap in the middle of the state. The people consider it large—is that not fitting?"
King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is there a way to interact with neighboring states?"
Mencius replied, "There is. Only the benevolent can take a great state and serve a small one—thus Tang served Ge, and King Wen served the Hunyi. Only the wise can take a small state and serve a great one—thus King Tai served the Xunyu, and Goujian served Wu. To take a great state and serve a small one is to delight in Heaven; to take a small state and serve a great one is to stand in awe of Heaven. Those who delight in Heaven preserve the world; those who stand in awe of Heaven preserve their state. The Odes say, 'Standing in awe of the majesty of Heaven, thus we preserve it.'"
The king said, "Great are these words! But I have a fault—I love valor."
Mencius replied, "I beg Your Majesty not to love small valor. A man who grasps his sword, glares fiercely, and says, 'How dare he stand against me!'—this is the valor of a common man, fit only to oppose a single foe. I beg Your Majesty to love great valor."
"The Odes say, 'The king blazed with anger, marshaled his hosts, to stop the march on Ju, to secure the blessings of Zhou, to answer the expectations of the world.' This was the valor of King Wen. With one burst of anger, King Wen brought peace to the people of the world."
"The Documents say, 'Heaven sent down the people below, appointing for them rulers and teachers. It is said they assist God, favoring the four quarters. Whether guilty or innocent, it is for me to decide. Who in the world dares to transgress his will?' One man acted violently in the world, and King Wu was ashamed of it. This was the valor of King Wu. And King Wu, too, with one burst of anger, brought peace to the people of the world. If now Your Majesty were to bring peace to the people of the world with one burst of anger, the people would only fear that Your Majesty does not love valor."
King Xuan of Qi met Mencius at the Snow Palace. The king said, "Do the worthy also have such pleasures?"
Mencius replied, "They do. If people cannot obtain such pleasures, they criticize their superiors. To be unable to obtain them and criticize one's superiors is wrong; but to be a ruler over the people and not share pleasures with them is also wrong. He who delights in the people's delights, the people will also delight in his delights. He who worries about the people's worries, the people will also worry about his worries. To delight and worry with the world—if one does not become king after this, it has never happened."
"In the past, Duke Jing of Qi asked Yanzi, 'I wish to travel to Zhuanfu and Chaowu, follow the coast southward, and reach Langya. How should I conduct myself to compare with the travels of the ancient kings?'"
"Yanzi replied, 'An excellent question! When the Son of Heaven visits the feudal lords, it is called a tour of inspection. A tour of inspection means inspecting what they guard. When the feudal lords come to court before the Son of Heaven, it is called reporting on duties. Reporting on duties means reporting on their responsibilities. There is never an occasion without purpose. In spring, they inspect the plowing and make up for deficiencies; in autumn, they inspect the harvest and aid those in need. A Xia proverb says, "If our king does not travel, how can we rest? If our king does not take pleasure, how can we be aided? One tour, one pleasure—this sets the standard for the feudal lords." Now it is not so: armies march and consume provisions, the hungry are not fed, the weary are not rested, all glare with resentment and slander each other, and the people turn to wickedness. To defy the mandate and oppress the people, to eat and drink as if flowing water, to indulge in wandering and excess—this worries the feudal lords. To drift downstream and forget to return is called "flowing"; to drift upstream and forget to return is called "lingering"; to hunt without satiety is called "excess"; to indulge in wine without satiety is called "ruin." The ancient kings had no pleasures of lingering and ruin, no conduct of excess. It is for you to choose your path.'"
"Duke Jing was pleased. He gave a great warning to the state, went out and lodged in the suburbs, and thereupon began to open the granaries and give aid to the deficient. He summoned the Grand Musician and said, 'Compose for me music about ruler and minister delighting in each other.' This was the music of Zhengzhao and Juezhao. The poem says, 'What fault is there in restraining the ruler? To restrain the ruler is to love the ruler.'"
King Xuan of Qi asked, "Everyone tells me to demolish the Bright Hall. Should I demolish it, or not?"
Mencius replied, "The Bright Hall is the hall of the king. If Your Majesty wishes to practice kingly government, then do not demolish it."
The king said, "May I hear about kingly government?"
Mencius replied, "In the past, when King Wen governed Qi, the farmers paid one-ninth of their produce, officials received hereditary salaries, customs and markets were inspected but not taxed, there were no prohibitions on ponds and weirs, punishment did not extend to the families of criminals, the old without wives were called widowers, the old without husbands were called widows, the old without children were called solitary, the young without fathers were called orphans. These four are the world's destitute and helpless. When King Wen enacted policies and practiced benevolence, he always put these four first. The Odes say, 'The rich may fare well, but pity the solitary and alone.'" The king said, "Excellent words!"
Mencius said, "If Your Majesty considers them excellent, why not put them into practice?"
The king said, "I have a fault—I love wealth."
Mencius replied, "In the past, Gong Liu loved wealth. The Odes say, 'He stored and filled the granaries, he wrapped up dry provisions. In bags and sacks, he thought to gather and use them gloriously. Bows and arrows were readied, shields, spears, and axes raised, and thus he began the march.' Thus, those who stayed had stored granaries, and those who marched had wrapped provisions—only then could they begin the march. If Your Majesty loves wealth, share it with the people—what difficulty would there be for you to become king?"
The king said, "I have a fault—I love beauty."
Mencius replied, "In the past, King Tai loved beauty and was fond of his consort. The Odes say, 'The ancient Duke Danfu came in the morning, galloping on his horse. Along the western banks of the river, he reached the foot of Mount Qi. With Lady Jiang, he came to inspect the dwellings.' In the time of this poem, there were no resentful women within, no unmarried men without. If Your Majesty loves beauty, share it with the people—what difficulty would there be for you to become king?"
Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi, "Suppose one of Your Majesty's ministers entrusted his wife and children to a friend and went to travel in Chu. When he returned, he found his wife and children cold and hungry. What should be done?" The king said, "Cast him off."
Mencius said, "If the chief judge cannot govern his subordinates, what should be done?" The king said, "Dismiss him."
Mencius said, "If the four borders of the state are not well-governed, what should be done?" The king looked left and right and spoke of other matters.
Mencius went to see King Xuan of Qi and said, "What is called an old state does not mean it has tall trees, but that it has ministers of long-standing service. Your Majesty has no intimate ministers. Those advanced in the past—today you do not know they are gone."
The king said, "How can I recognize the unworthy and dismiss them?"
Mencius said, "When a ruler advances the worthy, if it is unavoidable, he may cause the lowly to surpass the noble, the distant to surpass the intimate. Must he not be cautious? If all those around him say a man is worthy, it is not enough. If all the great officers say he is worthy, it is not enough. If all the people of the state say he is worthy, then investigate. If you find him worthy, then employ him. If all those around him say a man is unworthy, do not listen. If all the great officers say he is unworthy, do not listen. If all the people of the state say he is unworthy, then investigate. If you find him unworthy, then dismiss him. If all those around him say a man deserves death, do not listen. If all the great officers say he deserves death, do not listen. If all the people of the state say he deserves death, then investigate. If you find he deserves death, then put him to death. Thus it is said, 'The people of the state put him to death.' Only then can you be the father and mother of the people."
King Xuan of Qi asked, "Is it true that Tang banished Jie, and King Wu attacked Zhou?"
Mencius replied, "It is recorded as such." The king said, "Is it permissible for a minister to assassinate his ruler?"
Mencius said, "One who violates benevolence is called a thief; one who violates righteousness is called a tyrant. A thief and tyrant is called a mere fellow. I have heard of the execution of the fellow Zhou, but I have not heard of the assassination of a ruler."
Mencius said to King Xuan of Qi, "If you are building a great hall, you must have the master carpenter seek large timber. When the master carpenter obtains large timber, you are pleased and think him capable of his task. If the craftsmen cut it and make it small, you are angry and think him incapable. A man studies from youth and wishes to practice it in his prime. If you say, 'For now, set aside what you have learned and follow me,' what would that be like? Suppose there is an uncut jade here, even if it is worth ten thousand yi, you must have a jade worker carve and polish it. But when it comes to governing the state, you say, 'For now, set aside what you have learned and follow me.' How is this different from teaching a jade worker how to carve jade?"
The people of Qi attacked Yan and conquered it. King Xuan asked, "Some tell me not to take it, others tell me to take it. For a state of ten thousand chariots to attack another state of ten thousand chariots and conquer it in fifty days—human strength could not achieve this. If I do not take it, Heaven will surely send calamity. What about taking it?"
Mencius replied, "If taking it pleases the people of Yan, then take it. Among the ancients, there was one who did this—King Wu. If taking it does not please the people of Yan, then do not take it. Among the ancients, there was one who did this—King Wen. For a state of ten thousand chariots to attack another state of ten thousand chariots, and for the people to bring baskets of food and pots of drink to welcome your army—could there be any other reason? To escape from fire and water. If the water grows deeper and the fire hotter, they will simply turn elsewhere."
The people of Qi attacked Yan and took it. The feudal lords planned to rescue Yan. King Xuan said, "Many of the feudal lords are planning to attack me. How should I deal with them?"
Mencius replied, "I have heard that one who governed the world with seventy li was Tang. I have never heard of one with a thousand li who feared others. The Documents say, 'Tang's first campaign began with Ge. The world trusted him. When he campaigned east, the western barbarians complained; when he campaigned south, the northern barbarians complained. They said, "Why does he put us last?" The people looked to him as a great drought looks to clouds and rainbows. Those going to market did not stop, and farmers did not change. He punished their rulers and comforted their people, like timely rain falling. The people were greatly pleased.' The Documents say, 'We await our lord; when he comes, we will revive.' Now Yan oppresses its people. If Your Majesty campaigns against it, the people will think you are saving them from fire and water, and they will bring baskets of food and pots of drink to welcome your army. But if you kill their fathers and brothers, bind their sons and younger brothers, destroy their ancestral temples, and remove their precious vessels—how can this be permissible? The world already fears the strength of Qi. Now you double your territory without practicing benevolent government—this is to stir up the armies of the world. Your Majesty should quickly issue orders: return their old and young, stop the removal of their precious vessels, consult with the people of Yan, establish a ruler, and then withdraw. Then it may still be possible to stop the conflict."
Zou and Lu fought. Duke Mu asked, "Thirty-three of my officers died, yet none of the people died for them. If I punish them, I cannot punish them all; if I do not punish them, they will look on with hatred as their superiors die and not rescue them. What should I do?"
Mencius replied, "In years of famine and hardship, your people—the old and weak—fall into ditches and gullies, and the strong scatter to the four directions—nearly a thousand of them. Yet your granaries are full, your treasuries overflowing, and your officers do not report this. This is negligence above and cruelty below. Master Zeng said, 'Beware, beware! What comes from you will return to you.' The people have now gotten their chance to return it. Do not blame them. If you practice benevolent government, these people will love their superiors and die for their leaders."

段存义和马打了一辈子交道。
幼年时，他喂马养活了自己和弟弟；少年时，他驭马为自己挣得了一番前程；可人到中年……只因质疑御马管事人采买劣马，竟被诬陷勾结乱党，判处极刑……为保全自己与弟弟的性命，段存义妥协了——那位大人说，只要驭马让这座鎏金的巨舆驶向荒野，他便能活下去。
可是……他真的能活下去吗？
也罢，也好，既然开局贩马为生，结局也只能驭马向死。
秦地残月照影单，  

铁蹄销骨贩雕鞍。

马踏锦绡碎忠肝。
en:
Duan Cunyi has dealt with horses all his life. 
As a child, he fed horses to support himself and his younger brother. As a youth, he drove horses to earn himself a promising future. But in middle age... simply for questioning the horse master’s purchase of inferior steeds, he was falsely accused of conspiring with rebels and sentenced to death... To preserve his own and his brother’s lives, Duan Cunyi yielded, that official said if he would drive this gilded great carriage into the wilderness, he could live. 
But… would he truly survive? 
So be it. Since he began as a horse trader, he might as well end driving horses toward his death. 
A waning moon over Qin sheds light on a lonely shade,   

Iron hooves wear bones thin, once they sold carved saddles made.   

On crimson steps, a broken stirrup weaves the snare of crime,   

Steeds trample silk brocade, and shatter the loyal heart sublime.

被薛丑带出地下的时候，小六在笑，小七在哭，小八面无表情。
薛丑的障眼法，留住了阿爹的脸面，也留住了他们的命。但阿爹不会再要一把被人发现了破绽的武器。
就在他们并排跪在阿爹面前，不知命运如何的时候，薛丑提着一个破烂的布兜闯了进来。
他用一年的酒钱，换了他们的自由。

“我们无处可去。”小七在抽噎。
“我们想跟着你。”小六笑得谄媚。
“我们可以做你手中最锋利的那把刀。”小八郑重其事。
薛丑来来回回打量着他们，不过八九岁的女娃娃，名字起得敷衍，穿得破破烂烂，全身上下竟没一处好的。
“跟着我，也行……我正有一个大计。”
彼时恰逢新年，身后爆竹声连天，祝福声不断入耳。薛丑转了转手中空了的布兜。
“但先改个吉利的名字吧，叫……福禄寿，可好？”
en:
When Xue Chou led them out of the underground pits, Xiaoliu was grinning, Xiaoqi was sobbing, and Xiaoba's face remained blank.
His sleight of hand had spared their father's pride and their lives. But a weapon with exposed flaws would never be taken back.
As they knelt in a row before their father, awaiting their fate, Xue Chou barged in, swinging a tattered cloth bundle.
He'd traded a year's worth of liquor for their freedom.

"We have nowhere to go," Xiaoqi hiccuped between tears.
"We want to follow you," Xiaoliu simpered, her smile ingratiating.
"We can be the sharpest blade in your hand," Xiaoba declared solemnly.
Xue Chou eyed them one by one, three girls no older than nine, with hastily given names and threadbare clothes, not a single unbruised patch of skin between them.
"Fine, you can stay... I've got a grand plan brewing anyway."
Just then, New Year's fireworks erupted behind them, their booms mingling with distant cheers of celebration. Xue Chou spun the now-empty bundle on his finger.

zh:
【燕礼第六】

燕礼。小臣戒与者。膳宰具官馔于寝东。乐人县。设洗、篚于阼阶东南，当东霤。罍水在东，篚在洗西，南肆。设膳篚在其北，西面。司宫尊于东楹之西，两方壶，左玄酒，南上。公尊瓦大两，有丰，幂用綌若锡，在尊南，南上。尊士旅食于门西，两圆壶。司宫筵宾于户西，东上，无加席也。射人告具。
小臣设公席于阼阶上，西乡，设加席。公升，即位于席，西乡。小臣纳卿大夫，卿大夫皆入门右，北面东上。士立于西方，东面北上。祝史立于门东，北面东上。小臣师一人在东堂下，南面。士旅食者立于门西，东上。公降立于阼阶之东南，南乡尔卿，卿西面北上；尔大夫，大夫皆少进。
射人请宾。公曰：“命某为宾。”射人命宾，宾少进，礼辞。反命。又命之，宾再拜稽首，许诺，射人反命。宾出立于门外，东面。公揖卿大夫，乃升就席。
小臣自阼阶下，北面，请执幂者与羞膳者。乃命执幂者，执幂者升自西阶，立于尊南，北面，东上。膳宰请羞于诸公卿者。
射人纳宾。宾入，及庭，公降一等揖之。公升就席。
宾升自西阶，主人亦升自西阶，宾右北面至再拜，宾答再拜。主人降洗，洗南，西北面。宾降，阶西，东面。主人辞降，宾对。主人北面盥，坐取觚洗。宾少进，辞洗。主人坐奠觚于篚，兴对。宾反位。主人卒洗，宾揖，乃升。主人升。宾拜洗。主人宾右奠觚答拜，降盥。宾降，主人辞。宾对，卒盥。宾揖升。主人升，坐取觚。执幂者举幂，主人酌膳，执幂者反幂。主人筵前献宾。宾西阶上拜，筵前受爵，反位。主人宾右拜送爵。膳宰荐脯醢，宾升筵。膳宰设折俎。宾坐，左执爵，右祭脯醢，奠爵于荐右，兴；取肺，坐绝祭，哜之，兴加于俎；坐梲手，执爵，遂祭酒，兴；席末坐啐酒，降席，坐奠爵，拜，告旨，执爵兴。主人答拜。宾西阶上北面坐卒爵，兴；坐奠爵，遂拜。主人答拜。
宾以虚爵降，主人降。宾洗南坐奠觚，少进，辞降。主人东面对。宾坐取觚，奠于篚下，盥洗。主人辞洗。宾坐奠觚于篚，兴，对。卒洗，及阶，揖，升。主人升，拜洗如宾礼。宾降盥，主人降。宾辞降，卒盥，揖升，酌膳，执幂如初，以酢主人于西阶上。主人北面拜受爵，宾主人之左拜送爵。主人坐祭，不啐酒，不拜酒，不告旨；遂卒爵，兴；坐奠爵，拜，执爵兴。宾答拜。主人不崇酒，以虚爵降尊于篚。
……
en:
【The Sixth Ceremony of Yan】

The Ceremony of Yan. The minor steward warns the participants. The food officer arranges the officials' provisions east of the bedchamber. The musicians set up the bells and drums. A basin and basket are placed southeast of the eastern steps, aligned with the eastern eaves. The water jar is to the east, the basket west of the basin, facing south. The food basket is placed to its north, facing west. The palace steward places the wine vessels west of the eastern pillar: two square pots, with the dark wine on the left, arranged from the south. The duke's vessels are two large earthenware pots with stands, covered with coarse or fine cloth, placed south of the wine vessels, arranged from the south. The wine for the officers and retainers is placed west of the gate, in two round pots. The palace steward lays out the guest's mat west of the door, arranged from the east, without an additional mat. The archer announces that all is prepared.
The minor steward sets up the duke's mat on the eastern steps, facing west, with an additional mat. The duke ascends and takes his place on the mat, facing west. The minor steward ushers in the high ministers and great officers; they all enter from the right of the gate, facing north, arranged from the east. The officers stand in the west, facing east, arranged from the north. The invocators and scribes stand east of the gate, facing north, arranged from the east. One of the minor steward's assistants stands below the eastern hall, facing south. The officers and retainers stand west of the gate, arranged from the east. The duke descends and stands southeast of the eastern steps, facing south, and beckons the ministers; the ministers face west, arranged from the north. He beckons the great officers, and the great officers all step forward slightly.
The archer requests the guest. The duke says, "Appoint so-and-so as guest." The archer instructs the guest, who steps forward slightly and declines politely. The archer reports back. The duke instructs again, and the guest bows twice with his head to the ground, accepting. The archer reports back. The guest exits and stands outside the gate, facing east. The duke bows to the ministers and great officers, then ascends and takes his seat.
The minor steward, from below the eastern steps, facing north, requests the one to hold the cover and the one to present the food. He then instructs the one holding the cover, who ascends from the western steps and stands south of the wine vessels, facing north, arranged from the east. The food officer requests to present food to the various dukes and ministers.
The archer ushers in the guest. The guest enters and reaches the courtyard; the duke descends one step and bows to him. The duke ascends and takes his seat.
The guest ascends from the western steps, and the host also ascends from the western steps. The guest stands to the right of the host, facing north, and bows twice; the host returns the bow twice. The host descends to wash, standing south of the basin, facing northwest. The guest descends and stands west of the steps, facing east. The host declines the guest's descent, and the guest responds. The host washes his hands facing north, then kneels to take the goblet and rinse it. The guest steps forward slightly and declines the rinsing. The host kneels, places the goblet in the basket, rises, and responds. The guest returns to his position. The host finishes rinsing, and the guest bows, then ascends. The host ascends. The guest bows for the rinsing. The host, to the right of the guest, places the goblet down and returns the bow, then descends to wash his hands. The guest descends, and the host declines. The guest responds, and after washing, the guest bows and ascends. The host ascends, kneels, and takes the goblet. The one holding the cover lifts it, and the host pours the sweet wine; the one holding the cover replaces it. The host presents the goblet to the guest before the mat. The guest bows at the western steps, receives the goblet before the mat, and returns to his position. The host, to the right of the guest, bows and sends off the goblet. The food officer presents dried meat and pickled vegetables, and the guest ascends to the mat. The food officer sets up the carved meat platter. The guest kneels, holds the goblet in his left hand, and with his right hand offers the dried meat and pickled vegetables, places the goblet to the right of the offerings, and rises; he takes the lung, kneels, tears it as an offering, tastes it, rises, and places it on the platter; kneels, wipes his hands, takes the goblet, and then offers the wine, rises; at the end of the mat, he kneels, sips the wine, descends from the mat, kneels, places the goblet down, bows, declares the wine excellent, takes the goblet, and rises. The host returns the bow. The guest, at the western steps, facing north, kneels, drains the goblet, rises; kneels, places the goblet down, and bows. The host returns the bow.
The guest descends with the empty goblet, and the host descends. The guest kneels south of the basin, places the goblet down, steps forward slightly, and declines the host's descent. The host, facing east, responds. The guest kneels, takes the goblet, places it beneath the basket, and washes it. The host declines the washing. The guest kneels, places the goblet in the basket, rises, and responds. After washing, when reaching the steps, he bows and ascends. The host ascends and bows for the washing, as in the guest's ritual. The guest descends to wash his hands, and the host descends. The guest declines the host's descent, and after washing, bows, ascends, pours the sweet wine, and holds the cover as before, to toast the host at the western steps. The host, facing north, bows and receives the goblet; the guest, to the left of the host, bows and sends off the goblet. The host kneels and offers, does not sip the wine, does not bow for the wine, and does not declare it excellent; then drains the goblet, rises; kneels, places the goblet down, bows, takes the goblet, and rises. The guest returns the bow. The host does not press for more wine and descends with the empty goblet, placing it respectfully in the basket.
……

zh:
自打算把这里建成我的家乡时，我便种下了一片胡杨林。
这里也有了属于它的名字——胡杨集。
那个曾经注定飘荡的心，似乎也慢慢安定下来。
我开始熟悉胡杨集里、玉门关上每一个人的名字。
当然也包括那位将军。
将军多烦忧，有时也忧到胡杨集。他指着那几口一起修建的水井，说现在的胡杨集，很像河西。
仅仅是几口孤立的井，终有干涸的一日。
他想连通这里，勾连河西，直到大唐去。让这片大漠变为水草丰美的土地。
到那时，河西已复，玉门还于国土。
到那时，河西通往长安的商路重开，便让我再带着商队，光明正大地重走一次。

再后来，胡杨也慢慢长大，种子裹着飞絮，顺着商道传开了黄金乡的名字。
而我，攒着愈渐丰厚的家业，等着商队重走长安的一天。
en:
From the moment I resolved to make this place my home, I planted a grove of desert poplars.
And with them, a name took root: Poplar Bazaar.
My restless heart, once fated to wander, has slowly found its peace.
I came to know everyone in Poplar Bazaar and at Jade Gate Pass by name, including the general's.

He was a man of many worries, which often followed him here. Pointing to the wells we dug together, he said this place reminded him of Hexi—a string of lonely wells that would one day run dry.
His dream was to connect this oasis to Hexi and all the way to the heart of the Tang Empire, turning this desert into a land lush with water and grass.
On that day, he said, Hexi would be reclaimed, and Jade Gate Pass would return to the realm.
The trade routes to Chang'an would reopen, and I would lead my caravans down that road again, openly and with pride.

In time, the poplars grew tall. Their seeds, carried on the wind, spread the name of our golden home to lands far away.
As for me, I continue to build my fortune, waiting patiently for the day my caravan once again sets out for Chang'an.

en:
To my friend Xue Lin,

An urgent message has come from the Sect Master, bearing word that the fighting around the Hutuo River has grown dire. The dead and wounded lie everywhere, and healers are needed at once. We disciples of Silver Needle have already set out without delay. Yet the road north is long and the mountains many, while saving lives will not wait.
Lin, you always said you were no true physician, and so did not dare follow me into Silver Needle. You also said that the secret manual our master passed on to you was no proper art for healing. But when floodwaters break the dike, whether sand and stone, timber, or flesh and blood, all must be thrown in to hold the breach. So it is with any method that can stop the bleeding and save a life. Save them first. As for whatever troubles may follow, leave them all to me.
Forget talk of holy healers and miraculous hands. Anyone who can snatch a life back from death's edge is a physician of the highest order.

zh:
顺心每天的任务，就是跟着李小枸到处巡逻。在它心里，李小枸不是主人，是那个总爱口是心非的笨朋友。
朋友心里有话不敢说，小狗就要帮忙！明明不喜欢应酬，李小枸却假装要去喝酒；明明想听那人讲故事，嘴上却说“只是路过”。顺心不懂，为什么人总爱把真心话藏起来？
但没关系，顺心顺心，顺从本心！不想喝的酒，它就咬着裤腿把他拖走；想见的人，它就拽着衣角把他带过去。小狗听不懂人的弯弯绕绕，它只知道：想做的事就去做，想见的人就去见。
en:
Content's daily job is to trot after Li Xiaogou on patrol. In its eyes, Li Xiaogou isn't a master at all, just a clumsy friend who keeps saying the opposite of what he means.

When a friend has something to say but can't bring himself to say it, the dog has to help. He hates socializing, yet he puts on a show about going out for drinks. He wants to hear that person's stories, yet he insists he was "just passing by."

Content doesn't understand why humans hide what they really feel. But that's fine. Content is Content. It follows its heart.
If Li Xiaogou doesn't want that drink, Content bites his pant leg and drags him off. If he wants to see someone, Content tugs at his sleeve and pulls him over.

A dog doesn't get human roundabouts. It only knows this. If you want to do something, do it. If you miss someone, go see them.

zh:
【曲礼上第一】

曲礼曰：毋不敬，俨若思，安定辞，安民哉。
敖不可长，欲不可从，志不可满，乐不可极。
贤者狎而敬之，畏而爱之，爱而知其恶，憎而知其善，积而能散，安安而能迁，临财毋苟得，临难毋苟免，狠毋求胜，分毋求多，疑事毋质，直而勿有。
若夫，坐如尸，立如齐，礼从宜，使从俗。
夫礼者，所以定亲疏，决嫌疑，别同异，明是非也。礼不妄说人，不辞费。礼不逾节，不侵侮，不好狎。修身践言，谓之善行。行修言道，礼之质也。礼，闻取于人，不闻取人。礼闻来学，不闻往教。
道德仁义，非礼不成；教训正俗，非礼不备；分争辨讼，非礼不决；君臣上下，父子、兄弟，非礼不定；宦学事师，非礼不亲；班朝治军，莅官行法，非礼威严不行；祷祠祭祀，供给鬼神，非礼不诚不庄。是以君子恭敬、撙节、退让以明礼。鹦鹉能言，不离飞鸟；猩猩能言，不离禽兽。今人而无礼，虽能言，不亦禽兽之心乎？夫唯禽兽无礼，故父子聚麀。是故圣人作，为礼以教人，使人以有礼，知自别于禽兽。大上贵德，其次务施报。礼尚往来，往而不来，非礼也；来而不往，亦非礼也。人有礼则安，无礼则危。故曰：礼者，不可不学也。夫礼者，自卑而尊人，虽负贩者，必有尊也，而况富贵乎？富贵而知好礼，则不骄不淫；贫贱而知好礼，则志不慑。
人生十年曰幼，学；二十曰弱，冠；三十曰壮，有室；四十曰强，而仕；五十曰艾，服官政；六十曰耆，指使；七十曰老，而传；八十、九十曰耄；七年曰悼。悼与耄，虽有罪，不加刑焉。百年曰期，颐。大夫七十而致事，若不得谢，则必赐之几杖，行役以妇人，适四方，乘安车，自称曰老夫，于其国则称名。越国而问焉，必告之以其制。
谋于长者，必操几杖以从之。长者问，不辞让而对，非礼也。
凡为人子之礼，冬温而夏清，昏定而晨省，在丑夷不争。
夫为人子者，三赐不及车马，故州闾乡党称其孝也，兄弟亲戚称其慈也，僚友称其弟也，执友称其仁也，交游称其信也。见父之执，不谓之进不敢进，不谓之退不敢退，不问不敢对，此孝子之行也。
夫为人子者，出必告，反必面，所游必有常，所习必有业，恒言不称老。年长以倍，则父事之；十年以长，则兄事之；五年以长，则肩随之。群居五人，则长者必异席。
为人子者，居不主奥，坐不中席，行不中道，立不中门。食飨不为槩，祭祀不为尸。听于无声，视于无形。不登高，不临深，不苟訾，不苟笑。
孝子不服暗，不登危，惧辱亲也。父母存，不许友以死，不有私财。
为人子者，父母存，冠衣不纯素。孤子当室，冠衣不纯采。
幼子常视毋诳，童子不衣裘裳。立必正方，不倾听。长者与之提携，则两手奉长者之手，负剑辟，㖇诏之，则掩口而对。
……
en:
**"The Book of Rites: Qu Li, Part One"**

The Book of Rites says: Let there be no disrespect; let one's demeanor be grave, as if in deep thought; let one's words be settled and calm—this is how to bring peace to the people.
Arrogance must not be allowed to grow; desires must not be indulged; ambitions must not be fully satisfied; pleasures must not be pursued to their extreme.
For the worthy, be familiar yet respectful; stand in awe yet love them. Love them while knowing their faults; hate them while knowing their merits. Accumulate wealth yet be able to disperse it; dwell in comfort yet be able to move on. Faced with wealth, do not seek improper gain; faced with danger, do not seek to avoid responsibility. In conflict, do not strive solely for victory; in distribution, do not seek more than your share. In doubtful matters, do not insist on certainty; be straightforward, yet do not claim possession.
As for demeanor: sit as solemnly as a corpse in sacrifice; stand as respectfully as in a ceremony. Follow propriety according to what is fitting; follow customs when on missions.
Rites are what determine closeness and distance, resolve doubts and suspicions, distinguish similarities and differences, and clarify right and wrong. Rites do not flatter people recklessly, nor use excessive words. Rites do not overstep proper bounds, do not insult or bully, and do not delight in undue familiarity. Cultivating one's character and fulfilling one's words is called good conduct. Conduct that is cultivated and words that are in accordance with the Way—this is the essence of rites. It is said that rites are taken from others, not that they take others. It is said that one goes to learn rites, not that rites go to teach.
Virtue, morality, benevolence, and righteousness cannot be perfected without rites. Instruction, admonition, rectifying customs—these cannot be made complete without rites. Disputes, arguments, and litigations cannot be decided without rites. The relationships between ruler and minister, high and low, father and son, elder and younger brother—these cannot be fixed without rites. For officials and students serving their teachers, without rites there is no closeness. In arranging court audiences and governing the military, in overseeing officials and executing the law, without rites, authority and dignity cannot be established. In prayers, sacrifices, and offerings to spirits and deities, without rites, there is no sincerity and solemnity. Therefore, the noble man is reverent, restrained, and yielding to make rites clear. A parrot can speak, yet it does not leave the category of flying birds; a gibbon can speak, yet it does not leave the category of beasts. If a man today is without rites, though he can speak, is he not of the heart of beasts? It is precisely because beasts have no rites that fathers and sons share mates. Therefore, the sages arose and created rites to teach people, so that people, having rites, might know to distinguish themselves from beasts. The highest values virtue; the next strives for giving and repaying. Rites value reciprocity. To go and not come back is contrary to rites; to come and not go is also contrary to rites. A man with rites is secure; without rites, he is in peril. Therefore it is said: Rites are something one cannot but learn. Rites mean humbling oneself and honoring others. Even a porter or a peddler must have his dignity—how much more so the rich and noble? If the rich and noble know to love rites, they will not be arrogant or dissolute. If the poor and lowly know to love rites, their will will not be cowed.
At ten years of age, one is called a child and begins learning. At twenty, one is called weak and is capped. At thirty, one is called strong and takes a wife. At forty, one is called in one's prime and enters official service. At fifty, one is called Ai and takes on the duties of office. At sixty, one is called Qi and gives directions. At seventy, one is called old and hands over affairs. At eighty or ninety, one is called Mao. At seven years, one is called Dao. For Dao and Mao, even if they commit a crime, punishment is not applied. At one hundred years, one is called Qi, to be cared for. A high official retires at seventy. If he cannot be allowed to decline, he must be given a stool and a staff. When traveling on duty, he is accompanied by women. When going to the four quarters, he rides in a comfortable carriage. He refers to himself as "this old man." In his own state, he is called by his name. If someone from another state asks about him, he must be informed of the regulations concerning him.
When consulting with an elder, one must carry a stool and staff to follow him. If an elder asks a question, to answer without first declining is contrary to rites.
The rites for being a son: In winter, warm the parents' quarters; in summer, cool them. In the evening, settle them for the night; in the morning, inquire after their well-being. Among peers, do not contend.
For a son, even with three gifts, he should not accept carriages and horses. Thus, the villages and neighborhoods praise his filial piety; his brothers and relatives praise his kindness; his colleagues praise his fraternal respect; his close friends praise his benevolence; his acquaintances praise his trustworthiness. When he sees his father's close friend, if not told to advance, he dares not advance; if not told to withdraw, he dares not withdraw; if not asked, he dares not answer. This is the conduct of a filial son.
For a son: When going out, he must inform; when returning, he must present himself. His travels must have a regular pattern; his studies must have a proper focus. In ordinary speech, he does not refer to himself as old. For one twice his age, he serves him as a father. For one ten years older, he serves him as an elder brother. For one five years older, he walks shoulder-to-shoulder behind him. When five are sitting together, the elder must have a separate mat.
For a son: He does not occupy the main corner of the room; he does not sit in the middle of the mat; he does not walk in the middle of the path; he does not stand in the middle of the gateway. At feasts, he does not determine the portions; at sacrifices, he does not act as the representative corpse. He listens for what is not yet spoken; he sees what is not yet formed. He does not climb high; he does not approach depths; he does not criticize lightly; he does not laugh lightly.
A filial son does not serve in darkness, nor climb to dangerous heights, fearing to bring disgrace upon his parents. While parents are alive, he does not promise a friend to die for him, nor does he have private wealth.
For a son, while parents are alive, the trim of his cap and clothes is not pure white. An orphan who is head of the household, the trim of his cap and clothes is not pure color.
For a young child, constantly show him no deceit. A youth does not wear fur robes or skirts. He stands squarely, not leaning to listen. When an elder leads him by the hand, he receives the elder's hand with both hands. If the elder bends close to give instructions, he covers his mouth to reply.

When the general was still a boy, he carried many doubts in his heart.
Why were so many pieces of shattered armor from past generations enshrined in the Guo family ancestral hall?
Why did his father and uncle always make him practice writing the words "Chang'an"?
And why would his grandfather lie awake through the night over a single frontier report?
As the years passed, he walked farther down his path. He grew taller, and his understanding deepened.
He passed through Whitecrown Fortress, crossed Howling Sand Post, and went by Peaceward Camp. One day, he wrapped a cloth around a wounded commoner's injuries. When he finished and looked up, he met the person's gaze.
In that moment, the general realized that he finally understood.

zh:
“放生”，并非什么不传之秘。
据我所知，更久之前，很多养驼人都会一点“放生”。
不同人所用的“放生”流程也不同：有的要点燃红柳嫩芽，有的要将骆驼带到地矿裂缝处念诵药师经，有的要在驼峰上涂抹特定年份的盐。
神奇的是，他们几乎都能成功。
于是人们相信，“放生”能生效的根源是沙漠的感恩，仪式、道具都只是引动感恩之力的媒介。
但那都是沙暴出现之前的事了。
沙暴摧毁了太多东西，我已经很多年没看到过懂得“放生”的人了。
骆驼驿建成至今不到三年，我曾以为它也会是被沙暴轻易摧毁的事物之一。
老头第一次在骆驼驿“放生”骆驼那天，我喝光了一整坛好酒。
这世间有离合聚散，命途有生死周流，我们河西便是如此，每一个终点都会是新的起点。
巫术？不，那可是生命的威严呐。
en:
Releasing life is not some secret never passed on. 
From what I know, long ago, many camel herders knew a bit of this practice. 
Different people followed different rituals for "releasing life". some lit red willow shoots, some took camels to mineral cracks to recite the Medicine Buddha Sutra, some applied salt from specific years to the humps. 
Miraculously, almost all of them succeeded. 
Thus, people believed the root of the practice's effectiveness was the desert's gratitude, rituals and props were merely mediums to stir this power of gratitude. 
But that was all before the sandstorms appeared. 
Sandstorms have destroyed so much. I haven't seen anyone who knows how to "release life" in years. 
Camel Station has been built for less than three years. I once thought it would be just another thing easily destroyed by sandstorms. 
On the day the old man "released life" at Camel Station for the first time, I drank an entire jar of fine wine. 
The world is full of separations and reunions, life follows the cycle of birth and death. Such is Hexim every end is a new beginning. 
Witchcraft? No, that is the dignity of life.

他这个摊子说简陋也简陋——一张木桌，一顶破棚，旁边摆两个柳条筐，一个装肉丸，一个摞火烧。说讲究也讲究——那口锅他跑了四十里路，去镇上的铁匠铺蹲了整整一天，挨个敲了十七口锅才挑出来的。铁匠至今见了他还骂：“你个鳖孙，快把我敲聋了。”
他挑锅时手往锅底一拍，得听见“铛”的一声，要厚，要沉，要那股子声音从锅心荡到锅沿再弹回来才行。若是听着发空，他就摇头。
“漏底咧。”他把锅翻过来，指给铁匠看，“这儿，薄了一层。”
铁匠摸了半天没摸出来，气得胡子翘。
赵晓刚不管，他认准的事，十头牛也拉不回来。
这摊子在村口摆了三四个月，村里人就都认得他了。倒不是因为他的手艺——当然他的葱香肉丸确实紧实弹牙，烤肉火烧也确实外酥里嫩——而是因为他那嗓子吆喝，实在太怪了。
别人卖吃食，喊的是“香”“酥”“好吃不贵”。
而赵晓刚深吸一口气，额头的青筋也鼓起来：“大葱选硬挺咧——不要发软咧——”
这声拖得老长，顺着村道一路飘下去。
“小米选沙响咧——不要结蛋咧——”
“香稻选透亮咧——不要陈霉咧——”
最后一声，他必定拿铁勺往锅沿上敲一下。
“铛——”
“铁锅选厚实铛铛咧——不要漏底咧——”
行路人一头雾水，问村里人：“他这喊的啥？”
村里人就笑：“喊他自个儿的规矩哩。”
“规矩？”
“嗯。”村里人往摊子那边努努嘴，“这愣小子，料都是自己挑。葱要地里现拔的，专挑那杆子硬挺的，他说软塌塌的葱芯没魂儿。小米要搓一把听响，沙沙的才行，要是攥手里发黏结蛋，他扭头就走。那个香稻，你见过他蹲在村头粮铺一粒一粒对着日头照没有？一粒一粒照！老张头差点拿扫帚赶他。”
外村人听得咋舌：“这不一根筋么？”
“不一根筋，能做出这肉丸来？”
赵晓刚听见了，也不恼，闷头炸他的丸子。
面糊裹着葱肉馅儿，往油锅里一滑，滋啦一声，香味就顺着道窜出去。下地的人扛着锄头路过，肚子就叫了。他拿长筷子翻着，脸上被油烟气熏得发红，眼睛却亮得很。那双眼睛平常看着有点木，可一对着锅、对着料，就活了。
丸子炸到金黄，夹出来搁油纸上沥着。火烧从铁板那头铲过来，面饼烤得起了一层酥壳，拿刀剖开，塞进丸子，再抹一勺他自己调的酱。
递到人手里时，他也不说“慢用”，就说：“趁热。”
就两个字。
en:
The sky over Crownleek Terrace was still pitch black when a lone figure crouched by the dirt road.
Zhao Xiaogang was always here at this exact hour, like clockwork. He didn't even bother with a lantern. By the faint, fish-belly gray creeping over the eastern hills, he grabbed a handful of coarse salt and scrubbed his hands. He ground the grains into his skin again and again until his palms burned, scouring away every last speck of grease and dried dough. Only then did he wipe his hands on his apron and start setting up his stall.
At a glance, his setup was nothing special: a plain wooden table, a ratty awning, and two wicker baskets, one for meatballs, the other stacked with baked flatbreads. But look closer, and you'd see a man obsessed with the details. Take his iron wok. He'd hiked thirteen miles to the town blacksmith, squatted in the shop from dawn to dusk, and rapped his knuckles against seventeen different pots before finally picking one. To this day, the blacksmith still swore at him whenever they crossed paths: "You stubborn scoundrel, you nearly made me deaf!"
When testing a wok, Zhao would smack the bottom with his bare hand, listening for a very specific CLANG. It had to be thick and heavy. The sound had to ripple outward from the center, hit the rim, and bounce right back. If it sounded even a fraction hollow, he'd shake his head.
"It'll wear through," he'd say, flipping the heavy iron over to point at some invisible flaw. "Right here. It's a hair too thin."
The blacksmith would rub the spot for ages, feeling absolutely nothing, his beard twitching with rage. But Zhao couldn't care less. Once he dug his heels in, a herd of oxen couldn't drag him the other way.
He'd been setting up at the edge of the village for a few months now, and everyone knew who he was. It wasn't just his cooking, though his leek meatballs were perfectly springy, and his grilled meat buns were incredibly crispy on the outside and tender on the inside. No, he was famous because his street cries were just so weird.
Normal vendors shouted things like, "Hot and fresh!" or "Cheap and tasty!"
Zhao Xiaogang, on the other hand, would take a massive breath, the veins bulging on his forehead, and absolutely bellow:
"Leeks gotta be crisp and firm! No wilted greens!"
He'd drag that last syllable out, letting his voice carry all the way down the dirt road.
"Millet gotta rustle like sand! No clumpy grains!"
"Rice gotta be crystal clear! No moldy rot!"
And for his grand finale, he would always take his iron ladle and whack the rim of his wok.
CLANG!
"Iron woks gotta ring thick and true! No thin bottoms!"
Travelers passing through would look completely baffled. "What on earth is he yelling about?" they'd ask.
The locals would just laugh. "He's announcing his rules."
"Rules?"
"Yep." A villager would gesture toward the stall. "The kid is stubborn as a mule. He hand-picks every single ingredient. Leeks must be pulled fresh from the dirt, and he only takes the ones with stiff, rigid stalks. Says floppy leeks 'have no soul.' He tests his millet by rubbing a handful to see if it rustles like sand. If it feels even a little sticky, he walks away. And the rice. Have you seen him squatting outside the grain shop, holding the grains up to the sun? One by one! Elder Zhang nearly chased him off with a broom."
The traveler would stare in disbelief. "Isn't that taking it a bit far?"
"Maybe. But you think a sane man could make meatballs that taste like that?"
Zhao Xiaogang heard every word, but it didn't bother him. He just kept his head down and focused on his wok.
A scoop of batter-coated meat and leeks slid into the boiling oil with a vicious hiss. The savory aroma shot straight down the street, making the stomachs of passing farmers growl on the spot. Zhao worked the wok with a pair of extra-long wooden chopsticks. The greasy smoke flushed his face red, but his eyes were sharp and bright. Normally, the guy looked a little vacant, but the second he was standing over a hot stove, he came completely alive.
When the meatballs hit a perfect golden brown, he fished them out to drain on oiled paper. Then, he'd grab a baked flatbread off the griddle, toasted to a flaky, crackling crust, slice it open, stuff the sizzling meatballs inside, and smear the whole thing with a heavy spoonful of his homemade sauce.
When he handed the food over, he never bothered with polite customer service fluff like, "Enjoy your meal." He only ever gave a single, gruff instruction: "Eat it hot."

From the old dynasty to Kaifeng today, from the villages to the Imperial Artisan Court and Masterwood Hamlet, everyone praised Accountant Hu as a truly masterful human abacus.
With one glance, he could tell exactly how much timber a stool would need, how much stone a bridge would take, and how much material it would cost to build a peerless Quintadent Warship. By following his exact calculations, the artisans could craft an object without wasting a single sliver.
Working behind the scenes at Jinming Pool, Accountant Hu had counted labor, supplies, and funds, yet he had not counted on a fire that would reduce years of efforts to ashes.
"Alas, let it be..." Accountant Hu's eyes swept over the broken wood drifting with the current, the scattered wreckage, and a half-broken gear.
"Hey, hey!" Accountant Hu hurriedly patted the soldiers watching nearby. "Quick, fish it out! This can still be made into...
#Y[a small boat] The great warship may be gone, but it can still be made into a small boat. How convenient for ferrying across the river!"#E

What belongs to it is good. It loves to roll in the snow and even more to leap and snuggle close to people. 
You're warm, human. Not like me. 
After each hug, Snow Lion drifts into a long, deep sleep. Luckily, the snow on Wuwei Mountain never stops falling, so it will always wake again. 
No matter what, I just want a hug!

Then, suddenly, it was said she was the true mastermind, the butcher by the bedside. Later still, people remembered her name: Li, the Li of Tang. Yet the once-blossoming flower had vanished. She, together with those mysterious rumors, became an enigma without answer, impossible to know.

zh:
醉仙月的客房永远热热闹闹。小二为往来客人斟上离人泪，听五湖四海的侠客操着不同的口音讲着各地的见闻。但当他们饮尽杯中酒时，所有的语言都变成满足的喟叹。你突然想到，上次刀哥来不羡仙后，还没有坐在这里，喝上一壶你亲自斟满的酒。
有那样一把好刀的人，唯有世间的好酒才可相配。若是要去见刀哥，你定要准备一壶……
#Y葡萄酿。你曾在一场大梦中饮过凉州葡萄酿，那种甜而醉人的味道总让你贪饮几杯。不知道刀哥会如何评价，会不会说……这是小孩儿喝的？#E
你提着酒壶来到刀哥坟前，替他去了碑上的落叶。你记得在瓷窑初见时他的嘲讽，也记得在破庙中他的坦诚。你们说好一起要去江湖，去看看外面的世界。可他却像闯入你生活里的一场风暴，轰轰烈烈为你揭开了江湖的一角，然后便消散世间。是的，消散，如日光下的雪，似流水中的盐，无从搜寻。唯有一身怅然，尽付壶中酒。
en:
The Drunken Immortal Month is always bustling with life. The waiter pours Parting Tears for wanderers from all corners of the world, who are trading stories of their travels in varying accents. When they drain their cups, all words soften into contented sighs. You think of Blade's last visit and the cup you never poured for him.
A man with such a fine blade deserves only the finest wine in the world. If you are going to see Blade, you must prepare a pot of...
#YGrape Brew. You once drank Liangzhou Grape Brew in a dream; its sweet, heady flavor always made you crave a few extra cups. You wonder how Blade would judge it. Would he say... this is for children?#E
You bring a wine pot to Blade's grave and brush the fallen leaves from his tombstone. You remember his sneer when you first met at the porcelain kiln, and his blunt honesty in the ruined temple. You had agreed to venture into the jianghu together, to see the world outside. Yet he burst into your life like a fierce storm, dramatically tearing back a corner of the jianghu for you, only to vanish from this earth. Yes, he vanished, like snow under sunlight or salt in flowing water, nowhere to be found, leaving you with nothing but a deep sorrow, all poured into the wine in your pot.

唐文耀求教后协记：河北多三月下种，四、五月移栽秧苗，秧苗根硬后即勤除杂草。六月疏渠，保田中水量。至八月，水量可交替多寡。九月干田，颗粒归仓。

#Y刘思农批：写得好嘞。#E
en:
#YAutumn seed. Gather when dry. Keep high. Keep from damp...#E
Joint note after Sang Yu sought instruction: Seed gathered in winter should likewise be thoroughly sun-dried and always stored in a high place, to guard against ground moisture.

#YWinter wheat. Cover with straw. Keep roots safe.#E
Joint note after Tian Mo sought instruction: Wheat kept through the winter should be covered with dry straw. This protects the roots from frost and helps preserve the warmth of the soil.

#YThird month sow. Fourth month plant out. Fifth month weed. Sixth month clear channels. Seventh month water. Eighth month adjust water. Ninth month dry field.#E
Joint note after Tang Wenyao sought instruction: In Hebei, sowing is mostly done in the third month. In the fourth and fifth months, the seedlings are transplanted. Once the roots have hardened, the weeds must be cleared often. In the sixth month, the channels are opened to keep enough water in the fields. By the eighth month, the water level may be raised and lowered as needed. In the ninth month, the fields are dried and the grain brought in.

#YLiu Sinong's note: Well written.#E

zh:
饿。腹中空空，饥饿难耐。身上盘缠用尽，竟是连一块粗饼都买不起。
当街行乞，或与野狗夺食，眼下只余这两条出路。
路旁小摊中白面馒头刚刚出炉，只见店家高声吆喝。他望着那氤氲的雾气，心中几番纠结，还是没能放低身段去乞食。
思索过后，他找了处破庙歇息，意图用睡意来抵御腹中饥饿。昏沉间，却听见有人询问可否借此破庙歇息。他低声应过，复又转身睡去，总归这破庙也不是谁的地界。

待到天色变暗，他悠悠转醒。只见那人尚未离开，还在庙里燃起篝火来。那是个少年，仪表堂堂，眉宇间有几分正气。见他醒来，倒是没嫌弃他一身褴褛，还十分热情地邀他一道烤火。山中暮色沉沉，浸着几分凉意，他便没有推辞。
少年健谈，主动开口，说自己是往来江南江北的茶贩子。他低头看了眼身上的衣衫，并未接话。少年似是看穿了他的窘迫，指了指散落在地上的书籍与行囊。
“先生想必是个读书人，我最佩服读书人。”
“读书人最是无用。”他更觉惭愧，倒还不如就让少年当他是个乞丐。
“先生为何这样说？”少年有些疑惑。
“埋头苦读，辨不清世道，到头来只得栖身于破庙。”
“非也，世道不公，正是需得先生这样的读书人去改换，岂可安于这破庙。先生觉得是与不是？”
谈话间，少年从包中拿出最后一块粗饼，分出一半递给他。
他接过饼立马狼吞虎咽起来，心中亦有久违的激动，不知是太久没吃上一口东西还是因为方才少年说的话。
“在下姓柴，还不知先生名讳？”
“……，魏道济。”
en:
Empty. A gnawing, relentless emptiness. His last coin spent, he couldn't even afford a scrap of coarse bread.
Only two options remained: beg in the streets or fight stray dogs for scraps.
At a roadside stall, steam rose from freshly steamed buns. The vendor's cheerful hawking grated on his ears. He stared at the fragrant mist, pride and hunger warring within him, and in the end, he couldn't bring himself to stretch out a hand.
Defeated, he retreated to a dilapidated temple, hoping sleep might dull the ache. Half-conscious, he heard someone ask if they might share the space. He grunted assent and turned away. It wasn't as if he owned the place.

When he woke at dusk, the stranger was still there, a young man who'd lit a fire in the crumbling hall. Handsome, with an air of upright dignity, the youth didn't so much as blink at his tattered clothes, instead beckoning him warmly to the flames. The mountain evening carried a biting chill, so he didn't refuse.
The boy chattered freely, introducing himself as a tea merchant who traveled across the country. He glanced at his own threadbare sleeves and stayed silent. But the youth seemed to read his shame, nodding toward the books strewn nearby.
"You must be a scholar. I've always admired scholars."
"Scholars are useless." Bitter words. Better to be seen as a beggar.
"Why say that?" The youth doubted.
"Burying my head in books, blind to the world, and now I sleep in ruins."
"No," the youth said firmly. "An unjust world needs scholars like you to change it. How can you settle for this?"
As they spoke, the youth pulled out his last piece of flatbread and broke it in half.
He devoured his share ravenously. Was it the food or the youth's words that stirred him so?
"My surname is Chai. And yours?"
"...Wei Daoji."

今日得兴，现将毕生心血记录于此册，有缘人若得见且诚心实践，必将扶摇直上、前途一片光明啊！

其一，口舌之能，因人而异。
遇事不置可否，言必留三分余地。
若两派相争，当先叹"各有道理"，再私下对甲言"乙实咄咄逼人"，转而对乙道"甲未免刻薄"，但需注意，勿留话柄。待胜负既分，无论何方得势，皆可从容附之。
#Y旁注：......#E

其二，纵小敛大，进退有据。
治下当留无伤大雅之弊，有备无患，未雨绸缪。
如纵容下属略收小惠，待上官巡查时，即可大惊失色，捶胸顿足曰："下官失察，竟使宵小横行！"继而"痛心"自查，揪出无关紧要之下属，当众严惩以儆效尤。待上官面色稍霁，再趁机表功："幸赖大人明察，方使蠹虫现形。"如此既全上官威严，又保自身根基——须知剪除枝叶无伤根本，反倒愈显主干挺拔。

en:
For over thirty years, I have navigated the treacherous waters of official life, witnessing the endless twists and turns of fortune and fate. Those scholarly purists, who once prided themselves on unblemished virtue, have long since been banished to forgotten corners, while someone like me—pragmatic, clear-eyed, and adaptable—has steadily climbed the ranks. 
Today, in a rare moment of clarity, I commit the hard-won truths of my life to these pages. To whoever finds and truly heeds them, I promise a future radiant and full of promise. 

First, the art of speech lies in adaptability. 
Never bind yourself to a single stance; always leave a margin for retreat. 
When factions clash, begin by acknowledging, "Both sides have their merits." Then, in private, gently confide to Party A that Party B can be overbearing, and to Party B that Party A is somewhat harsh. But be careful never to leave words that could be twisted against you. When the dust settles and power shifts, you can easily align yourself with the new victor, moving like water conforming to every shape. 
#YSide note: ... #E

Second, tolerate small faults to prevent larger ones. 
Allow minor, harmless transgressions under your watch—they will serve you well later. 
Let a subordinate collect small bribes. When your superior arrives unannounced, feign shock and sorrow: "I have failed my duty and allowed corruption to spread!" Then, with feigned heartache, root out a minor, insignificant official and make a public example of him. Once your superior's anger subsides, seize the moment to praise his wisdom: "Thanks to your keen oversight, the vermin were uncovered." In doing so, the dignity of your superior remains intact, and your own position strengthens. Pruning twigs does not harm the tree—instead, it makes the trunk appear all the more robust. 
#YSide note: Seems to make sense, doesn't it? #E

Third, pursue gain, avoid blame, and protect your reputation. 
Be the first to claim success; the last to admit failure. 
If a task falls apart and you face accusations, begin by expressing heartfelt regret. Wipe away tears, choke back emotions, then lament, "Everyone made mistakes," subtly casting blame on others without ever implicating yourself. Thus, someone else will shoulder the burden. 

Fourth, accept gifts under a veil of refinement. 
If you must receive gratuities, cloak them in culture and grace. 
When a merchant offers a "family heirloom painting," respond solemnly, "Such a treasure belongs in the public collection." If a wealthy patron presents a rare manuscript, sigh and say, "I will safeguard this precious volume for now." Should inquiries arise, point to your shelves full of "items held in trust," earning you a reputation for nurturing talent instead of greed. 
#YSide note: Ah, so that's how the game is played!#E 
... 
Seventy-two such principles in all—each word born from experience, every sentence a beacon of wisdom. 
Ultimately, the path of an official boils down to two qualities: keen wit and subtle perception. Without the might to move mountains or the courage to face armies alone, to rise amid a den of wolves, one must master the fine art of cunning. 

#YSide note: If I follow these rules to the letter, will I truly ascend, step by steady step?#E 
#YWill my hopes come to bloom and all desires be fulfilled?#E 
#YAnd what if one possessed the mighty strength—would these stratagems still matter?#E

如是我闻，一时佛在室罗筏城，祇桓精舍。与大比丘众，千二百五十人俱。皆是无漏大阿罗汉，佛子住持，善超诸有；能于国土，成就威仪 ；从佛转轮，妙堪遗嘱；严净毗尼，弘范三界；应身无量，度脱众生；拔济未来，越诸尘累。其名曰：大智舍利弗、摩诃目犍连、摩诃拘絺罗、富楼那弥多罗尼子、须菩提、优婆尼沙陀等，而为上首。复有无量辟支无学，并其初心，同来佛所 ，属诸比丘，休夏自恣。十方菩萨，咨决心疑，钦奉慈严，将求密义。即时如来，敷座宴安，为诸会中，宣示深奥，法筵清众，得未曾有。迦陵仙音，遍十方界。恒沙菩萨 ，来聚道场，文殊师利，而为上首。
……
en:
Volume I
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, at the Jetavana Grove, with a great assembly of 1,250 bhikṣus. All were arhats, free from defilement, disciples upheld by the Buddha, transcending all existence; majestic in conduct, they upheld the Dharma, turning the wheel with the Buddha, worthy of his sacred charge. Stern in vinaya, they were models across the Three Realms; with boundless manifested forms, they liberated beings, delivering the future beyond worldly burdens. Present were Mahāprajñā Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāli, and others, leading the assembly. Also present were countless pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, along with those newly resolved, all gathered before the Buddha as the bhikṣus concluded their summer retreat. Bodhisattvas from the ten directions sought resolution to their doubts, revering the Compassionate and Stern One, yearning for esoteric truths. Then the Tathāgata, seated serenely, expounded profound doctrines to the assembly. The pure gathering at this Dharma feast witnessed the unprecedented. The kalaviṅka's divine voice filled the ten directions. Bodhisattvas as numerous as Ganges' sands converged upon the dais, with Mañjuśrī at their head.

zh:
维年月日，清河乡民王大生具清酌之奠，告李兄存之灵：
呜呼！闻兄殁时，年尚三旬，所怀高义，深于此河。阿兄与吾有总角之好，情似手足。兄长家贫，吾家时济以余粮；不过滴水，阿兄常怀涌泉之心。吾尝犯法，兄虽为胥吏，却以身匿弟。县尉究之，终不言弟所在。县尉言：“贼在汝膝下。”兄持石自击其膝盖，曰：“贼安在？”复以火灼兄，兄呼：“凉！凉！”左右之人，皆不忍视。县尉寻吾不得，明府判兄流千里。
呜呼！忽得远信，悲报骤来。不过二载，兄竟身死他乡，百年之后，弟岂独葬故土。虽哀恸之至，吾即启程，敛兄遗骨。清河水长，明灯不熄，阿兄归哉！呜呼！尚飨！
en:
On this day of mourning, Qinghe villager Wang Dasheng offers pure wine in libation and speaks to the spirit of Brother Li: 
Alas! When you departed, you were but thirty years of age, yet your righteousness ran deeper than this river. You and I were childhood friends, closer than brothers. Though your family was poor, mine often shared our surplus grain with yours, mere drops of aid, yet you repaid them with the heart of a surging spring. When I broke the law, though you served as a clerk, you hid me at great peril. The county captain interrogated you, but you never revealed my whereabouts. "The criminal is beneath your knees," the captain said. You took a stone and struck your own kneecap, demanding, "Where is he now?" When they burned you with fire, you cried out, "Cool! So cool!" Those who witnessed it could not bear to look. The captain never found me, but the magistrate sentenced you to exile a thousand li away.
Alas! Then came the distant letter, the sudden news of grief. Within two years, you perished in a foreign land. A hundred years hence, how can I let you lie buried alone, far from home? Though grief rends me, I journey now to bring your bones home. May Qinghe's endless waters light your way. Partake, dear brother, of this final offering.

于开山事分歧弥深，鸦与青终是道殊。前巨子鸦栖隐乡野，于碧水云涛结庐，广收弟子，设塾授经，启智童蒙。及鸦先生殁，诸弟子年幼，悉送归墨城。然传言其藏秘宝于谷中，或可登九天，平山海。
穷奇师素怀异志，遽率众据谷，封山锁径，昼夜搜掘，仍无所获。时有三狡童，身虽稚弱，志却坚毅，潜行而至，匿身桃林，誓护先生所遗秘宝。
后之来者，若有慧心，或可拨雾见真，寻得所藏。
en:
The former Grandmaster Raven retreated into the wilderness, settling in the Jadestream Valley. There, he built a hut as a school and taught the classics to enlighten the young. When he passed, his young disciples were sent back to Mohist City. Yet, rumors spread about a treasure Grandmaster Raven had hidden in the valley, said to grant the power to soar to the heavens and calm the wildest of seas.
The Qiongqi Artificers, harboring dark ambitions, suddenly seized the valley. They sealed the paths and dug day and night, yet found nothing. Meanwhile, three clever children slipped in unnoticed. They vanished among the Peach Grove, pledging to guard the master's sacred legacy.
For those who follow, endowed with sharp insight and courage, the mists may part to reveal the valley's truth and unlock its hidden wonders.

en: Watching them calls to mind the ancient Chancellor Li Si, and his famous parable of the rats: one starving in a filthy latrine, the other feasting fearlessly in a granary. Chasing that granary, he climbed to the very pinnacle of the empire, only to be executed by the Second Emperor. In his final moments, he wept, wishing only that he could lead his hunting dog out the eastern gates of his hometown one last time. Had Li Si seen the squirrels of West Lake, he surely would have traded his courtly robes for the life of a modestly wealthy man, living quietly among the lakes and mountains. Yet, wealth must have its limits. When a squirrel grows too fat, it loses its lightning grace and becomes an easy mark for the circling falcon. 《玉篇》有云，“骁勇也。”骠，马行疾貌，又指毛色中夹杂点点斑纹。乌孙西极中有此纹理者，为金骠。
西汉武帝年间，西域有古国乌孙，不务农耕，以游牧为生，地产良马。《汉书·张骞传》记载：“骞既至乌孙，致赐谕指……乌孙发译道送骞，与乌孙使数十人，马数十匹，报谢，因令窥汉，知其广大。”张骞出使西域，将乌孙骏马带回中原，汉武帝见乌孙马神骏非凡，欣喜万分，名曰“西极”。
乌孙西极体格魁伟，四肢强健，头颅小巧，耳短眸清，外形俊秀。性温顺，耐粗放，春夏时节食草增膘，秋冬时节亦能刨雪觅食，力速兼备，挽乘皆宜，为西域特有的良马马种。
en:
The Jade Book states, "Fierce and brave." Biao describes a swift-moving horse with small spots scattered through its coat. Wusun Western Rarities bearing this pattern are called Jinbiao.
During Emperor Wu of the Western Han, the nomadic state of Wusun in the Western Regions was famed for its fine horses.
As recorded in the Book of Han, Biography of Zhang Qian, "Upon arrival in Wusun Kingdom, Zhang Qian delivered imperial gifts...the state dispatched envoys and gifted dozens of horses in return to detect the vastness of Western Han." Zhang Qian brought Wusun steeds back to the Central Plains. Emperor Wu, impressed by their spirit and beauty, named them "Western Rarity".
Wusun Western Rarities are large and powerful, with well-shaped limbs, small heads, short ears, and bright eyes. Gentle in nature and hardy by breed, they fattened easily in summer pastures and foraged even through winter snow. Strong and swift, they served equally well for riding or dragging, an exceptional breed unique to the Western Regions.

【尽心章句下】

孟子曰：不仁哉，梁惠王也！仁者以其所爱及其所不爱，不仁者以其所不爱及其所爱。公孙丑曰：何谓也？
“梁惠王以土地之故，糜烂其民而战之，大败。将复之，恐不能胜，故驱其所爱子弟以殉之，是之谓以其所不爱及其所爱也。
孟子曰：春秋无义战。彼善于此，则有之矣。征者，上伐下也。敌国不相征也。
孟子曰：尽信书则不如无书。吾于武成，取二三策而已矣。仁人无敌于天下，以至仁伐至不仁，而何其血之流杵也？
孟子曰：有人曰：我善为陈，我善为战，大罪也。国君好仁，天下无敌焉。南面而征，北夷怨；东面而征，西夷怨，曰：奚为后我？武王之伐殷也，革车三百两，虎贲三千人。王曰：无畏，宁尔也，非敌百姓也。若崩厥角，稽首。征之为言正也，各欲正己也，焉用战？
孟子曰：梓匠轮舆，能与人规矩，不能使人巧。
孟子曰：舜之饭糗茹草也，若将终身焉。及其为天子也，被袗衣，鼓琴，二女果，若固有之。
孟子曰：吾今而后知杀人亲之重也，杀人之父，人亦杀其父；杀人之兄，人亦杀其兄。然则非自杀之也，一閒耳。
孟子曰：古之为关也，将以御暴；今之为关也，将以为暴。
孟子曰：身不行道，不行于妻子；使人不以道，不能行于妻子。
孟子曰：周于利者，凶年不能杀；周于德者，邪世不能乱。
孟子曰：好名之人能让千乘之国。苟非其人，箪食豆羹见于色。
孟子曰：不信仁贤则国空虚，无礼义则上下乱，无政事则财用不足。
孟子曰：不仁而得国者，有之矣。不仁而得天下，未之有也。
孟子曰：民为贵，社稷次之，君为轻。是故得乎丘民而为天子，得乎天子为诸侯，得乎诸侯为大夫。诸侯危社稷则变置。牺牲既成，粢盛既絜，祭祀以时，然而旱乾水溢，则变置社稷。
孟子曰：圣人，百世之师也。伯夷、柳下惠是也。故闻伯夷之风者，顽夫廉，懦夫有立志。闻柳下惠之风者，薄夫敦，鄙夫宽。奋乎百世之上，百世之下闻者莫不兴起也。非圣人而能若是乎？而况于亲炙之者乎？
孟子曰：仁也者，人也。合而言之，道也。
