zh: 原唐教坊曲名，后用作词调名。此调有不同诸格体，俱为双调。李群玉《留别马使君》：“唯有管弦知客意，分别吹出《感恩多》”。白居易《闻歌伎唱严郎中诗》：“但是人家有遗爱，就中苏小感恩多”。此曲传至东瀛后亦有流变，《大日本史》列《感恩多》在平调，又入乞食调或性调。
en: Originally a title from Tang imperial music, this tune exists in several forms, many of them classified as double tunes. Li Qunyu's Parting with Magistrate Ma reads: "Only the strings understand the guest's feelings, clearly playing Gratitude in farewell." Bai Juyi's Hearing a Singing Girl Perform Yan's Work notes: "Yet she left behind the love of others; among them, Su Xiaoxiao felt the deepest gratitude." After the tune was introduced to Japan, it likewise underwent adaptation. The History of Great Japan records Gratitude in the Heijo mode, and it is also catalogued under other modal systems such as Kojiki and Sei.

zh:
窥天其一策，以已知之事衍未至之事，是为天衍。
自有此窥天计，历代先贤凝智、又屡得孤云相助，方得此算阵，欲晓天裂之变，推造化万机。
先有开运年间，算得太白山崩，近又算得天下洪害。皆传信于外，略尽薄力。
飞天千载事，天衍亦如此。所托之人，须思之甚慎。
我遍后辈俊杰，万师天资有余，而心性不坚。启蛰筹谋虽多，其虑颇多牵绊。
唯青儿心志如磐，虽不擅精工机巧，却于枢机规设一道颇有见解。
不独如此，此前与青儿论“水中捞月”，青儿答曰：天下道与术，缺一则不全。道者如树木之根，术者如冠上之叶。根不固则叶易枯，叶不繁则树犹死。
先有前人具“捞月”之心，承“捞月”之术。才有后人继“捞月”之志，得“摘月”之功。
那日青儿走后，已是三更。低头可见明月映碧水，抬头又见天朗气清，明月天边。
心下畅快，乃沽浊酒一壶，与巨子鹔修书一封。
en:
One method of peering into Heaven is to infer what has not yet come to pass from what is already known. This is called Heavenly Reckoning.
Since this art first began, generations of predecessors have poured their wisdom into it, aided time and again by Lone Cloud. Only thus was this calculating array brought into being, to probe the rifts of Heaven and reckon the myriad workings of creation.
In the Kaiyun years, it foretold the collapse of Mount Taibai. More recently, it foretold the great floods that would afflict the realm. In both cases, warnings were sent out, and what little strength we had was put to use.
To fly to Heaven is a work of a thousand years. In this as in all else, the one entrusted with it must be chosen with the utmost care.
I have looked over the promising talents of the younger generation. Wanshi has gifts enough, yet his resolve is not firm. Qizhe is rich in plans and devices, yet his thoughts are burdened by too many ties.
Only Halcyon is steadfast as stone. Though not especially gifted in the finest crafts of mechanism, she shows uncommon insight when it comes to the ordering of pivots and the principles of design.
More than that, when I once spoke with Halcyon of fishing the moon from the water, she answered:
"In all things under Heaven, principle and craft are both indispensable. Principle is like the root of a tree, craft like the leaves in its crown. If the root is not firm, the leaves soon wither. If the leaves do not flourish, the tree too will die.
It was because those who came before held the will to fish for the moon, and handed down the craft of fishing for the moon, that those who came after could inherit that same will, and in time achieve the deed of drawing down the moon."
By the time Halcyon took her leave that day, it was already the third watch. Lowering my head, I saw the bright moon mirrored in the green water. Raising it again, I found the sky clear and open, with the moon hanging at Heaven's edge.
At once my heart grew light. So I bought a jug of rough wine and wrote a letter to Grandmaster Osprey.

【器用·三】

【画】

当涂赵炎少府粉图山水歌
李白
峨眉高出西极天，罗浮直与南溟连。
名公绎思挥彩笔，驱山走海置眼前。
满堂空翠如可扫，赤城霞气苍梧烟。
洞庭潇湘意渺绵，三江七泽情洄沿。
惊涛汹涌向何处，孤舟一去迷归年。
征帆不动亦不旋，飘如随风落天边。
心摇目断兴难尽，几时可到三山巅。
西峰峥嵘喷流泉，横石蹙水波潺湲。
东崖合沓蔽轻雾，深林杂树空芊绵。
此中冥昧失昼夜，隐几寂听无鸣蝉。
长松之下列羽客，对坐不语南昌仙。
南昌仙人赵夫子，妙年历落青云士。
讼庭无事罗众宾，杳然如在丹青里。
五色粉图安足珍，真仙可以全吾身。
若待功成拂衣去，武陵桃花笑杀人。

丹青引赠曹将军霸
杜甫
将军魏武之子孙，于今为庶为清门。
英雄割据虽已矣，文采风流今尚存。
学书初学卫夫人，但恨无过王右军。
丹青不知老将至，富贵于我如浮云。
开元之中常引见，承恩数上南熏殿。
凌烟功臣少颜色，将军下笔开生面。
良相头上进贤冠，猛将腰间大羽箭。
褒公鄂公毛发动，英姿飒爽来酣战。
先帝天马玉花骢，画工如山貌不同。
是日牵来赤墀下，迥立阊阖生长风。
诏谓将军拂绢素，意匠惨澹经营中。
斯须九重真龙出，一洗万古凡马空。
玉花却在御榻上，榻上庭前屹相向。
至尊含笑催赐金，圉人太仆皆惆怅。
弟子韩幹早入室，亦能画马穷殊相。
幹惟画肉不画骨，忍使骅骝气凋丧。
将军画善盖有神，偶逢佳士亦写真。
即今漂泊干戈际，屡貌寻常行路人。
途穷反遭俗眼白，世上未有如公贫。
但看古来盛名下，终日坎壈缠其身。

相和歌辞·团扇郎
刘禹锡
团扇复团扇，奉君清暑殿。
秋风入庭树，从此不相见。
上有乘鸾女，苍苍虫网遍。
明年怀袖中，谁见机中练。

素是自然色，圆因裁制功。
飒如松起籁，飘似鹤翻空。
盛夏不销雪，终年无尽风。
引秋生手里，藏月入怀中。
麈尾斑非疋，蒲葵陋不同。
何人称相对，清瘦白须翁。

画扇

en:
【Implements · Three】

【Painting】

Song of the Painted Landscape by Zhao Yan, Assistant Magistrate of Dangtu
Li Bai
Mount Emei towers to the western sky's height,
Luofu connects to the Southern Sea's might.
A master's mind wields the brush with great art,
Driving mountains and seas before the heart.
The hall is filled with an emerald hue so clear,
Red walls' mist and Cangwu's smoke appear.
Dongting and Xiaoxiang stretch vague and far,
Three rivers, seven marshes, near and far.
Where do the raging waves fiercely go?
A lone boat departs, lost, no return to show.
The sail hangs still, neither turning nor flown,
Drifting like wind to the sky's edge alone.
Heart swaying, gaze lost, joy hard to contain,
When will I reach the three peaks' domain?
Western peaks tower, gushing springs cascade,
Rocks block the stream, where rippling waves are made.
Eastern cliffs are veiled in light mist's embrace,
Deep woods with trees in a lush, empty space.
Here, darkness blurs the line of night and day,
Leaning on desk, in silence, cicadas stay.
Beneath tall pines, feather-robed guests convene,
Sitting in silence, Nanchang's immortal scene.
Nanchang's immortal, Master Zhao by name,
In youth, a lofty scholar of noble fame.
His court at peace, guests gather without strife,
As if within a painting, free from life.
What use are colored sketches, fine and grand?
True immortals can preserve us, hand in hand.
If one waits for success to shed worldly ties,
Wuling's peach blossoms mock with laughing eyes.

Song of Painting, Presented to General Cao Ba
Du Fu
A general, descendant of Wei's martial line,
Now a commoner, of humble design.
Though heroes' divided rule is past and gone,
Their literary grace and spirit linger on.
First learning calligraphy from Lady Wei,
Yet regretting not surpassing Wang's decree.
Painting unaware of aging's approach,
Wealth and honor like fleeting clouds encroach.
In Kaiyuan's reign, often summoned to appear,
Receiving grace at South Fragrance Hall, dear.
Lingyan's heroes had faded hues so slight,
The general's brush revived them with new light.
Wise ministers wore caps of virtue high,
Fierce generals with great feathered arrows nigh.
Duke Bao and Duke E, hair and beard alive,
In heroic stance, ready to strive.
The late emperor's steed, Jade Flower Crown,
Painters like hills, yet none could capture renown.
That day led beneath the red steps' domain,
Standing tall at Changhe, stirring wind's train.
Edict ordered the general to prepare silk white,
With careful thought, in deep design's twilight.
In moments, a true dragon from nine heavens springs,
Washing away all common horses' things.
Jade Flower seems upon the royal bed to stay,
On bed and court, facing each other, they sway.
The sovereign smiles, urging gold to bestow,
Grooms and stewards in dismay and sorrow.
Disciple Han Gan, early entered the room,
Could paint horses in every form and gloom.
Gan painted flesh but not the bone within,
Letting Hua Liu's spirit grow sadly thin.
The general's paintings, divine in their art,
Meeting fine scholars, portraits from the start.
Now drifting in times of strife and war's plight,
Often sketching ordinary folks in sight.
At road's end, met with common eyes' disdain,
In all the world, none as poor remain.
But look at those of ancient, famed renown,
All day by hardship and misfortune bound.

【Fan】

Ballad of the Round Fan
Liu Yuxi
Round fan, oh round fan, in your hand,
Served in the Clear Summer Hall, so grand.
Autumn wind enters the courtyard tree,
From this moment, we shall no longer see.
Upon it, a maiden rides a phoenix high,
Covered in gray spiderwebs, she lies.
Next year within the sleeve it's kept,
Who will see the loom's cloth, adept?

White Feather Fan
Bai Juyi
Plain is its natural hue,
Round from crafting, skilled and true.
Rustling like pines in whispered sound,
Floating like cranes in skyward bound.
In midsummer, snow never melts away,
Endless wind throughout the year to sway.
Bringing autumn to the hand's embrace,
Hiding moonlight in a secret space.
Deer-tail tassels, unmatched in grace,
Palm-leaf fans, a lesser place.
Who can face it, pair with art?
A thin, white-bearded elder, apart.

Painted Fan
Li Shangyin
Do not bring the painted fan past the screen,
To veil spring hills and stall talent's sheen.
If said to be round like the bright moon's face,
Here must osmanthus bloom in its place.

To the Esteemed Swordsman,
Recently, everyone in Kaifeng Prefecture has been on edge, and the reason is—
Cats.
Yes, cats. You must be wondering, how could a few cats bring Kaifeng Prefecture to its knees? Well, guess what—these past few days, whenever anyone steps out, cats have been tugging at their robes, dragging the officials here. What's here? I wanted to know too, so I followed along, and guess what? You're here!
Seeing you unconscious, our military advisor, in his ignorance, summoned a Taoist priest named Wang who supposedly understands cat language. The priest said these cats want their Meow Meow Coins, which you're lying on.
Isn't that strange? These days, cats can report to the authorities, humans can talk to cats, and some can sleep so deeply without moving a muscle. But you clearly look like a Great Hero who roams the martial world. Matters of the martial world are not for us to pry into, so we’ll leave it to you. The cats here, wise as they are, will deliver this letter. A small gift is enclosed, hoping it aids your journey. Feel free to drop by Kaifeng Prefecture for tea anytime!

zh:
【丧大记第二十二】

疾病，外内皆扫。君大夫彻县，士去琴瑟。寝东首于北墉下。废床。彻亵衣，加新衣，体一人。男女改服。属纩以俟绝气。男子不死于妇人之手，妇人不死于男子之手。君夫人卒于路寝，大夫世妇卒于适寝，内子未命，则死于下室。迁尸于寝，士士之妻皆死于寝。
复，有林麓，则虞人设阶；无林麓，则狄人设阶。小臣复，复者朝服。君以卷，夫人以屈狄；大夫以玄赪，世妇以襢衣；士以爵弁，士妻以税衣。皆升自东荣，中屋履危，北面三号，卷衣投于前，司服受之，降自西北荣。其为宾，则公馆复，私馆不复；其在野，则升其乘车之左毂而复。复衣不以衣尸，不以敛。妇人复，不以袡。凡复，男子称名，妇人称字。唯哭先复，复而后行死事。
始卒，主人啼，兄弟哭，妇人哭踊。既正尸，子坐于东方，卿大夫父兄子姓立于东方，有司庶士哭于堂下北面；夫人坐于西方，内命妇姑姊妹子姓立于西方，外命妇率外宗哭于堂上北面。大夫之丧，主人坐于东方，主妇坐于西方，其有命夫命妇则坐，无则皆立。士之丧，主人父兄子姓皆坐于东方，主妇姑姊妹子姓皆坐于西方。凡哭尸于室者，主人二手承衾而哭。
君之丧，未小敛，为寄公国宾出；大夫之丧，未小敛，为君命出；士之丧，于大夫不当敛而出。凡主人之出也，徒跣扱衽拊心，降自西阶。君拜寄公国宾于位；大夫于君命，迎于寝门外，使者升堂致命，主人拜于下；士于大夫亲吊则与之哭；不逆于门外，夫人为寄公夫人出，命妇为夫人之命出，士妻不当敛，则为命妇出。
小敛，主人即位于户内，主妇东面，乃敛。卒敛，主人冯之踊，主妇亦如之。主人袒说髦，括发以麻，妇人髽，带麻于房中。彻帷，男女奉尸夷于堂，降拜：君拜寄公国宾，大夫士拜卿大夫于位，于士旁三拜；夫人亦拜寄公夫人于堂上，大夫内子士妻特拜，命妇泛拜众宾于堂上。主人即位，袭带绖踊。母之丧，即位而免，乃奠。吊者袭裘，加武带绖，与主人拾踊。君丧，虞人出木角，狄人出壶，雍人出鼎，司马县之，乃官代哭，大夫官代哭不县壶，士代哭不以官。君堂上二烛、下二烛，大夫堂上一烛、下二烛，士堂上一烛、下一烛。宾出彻帷。哭尸于堂上，主人在东方，由外来者在西方，诸妇南乡。妇人迎客送客不下堂，下堂不哭；男子出寝门见人不哭。其无女主，则男主拜女宾于寝门内；其无男主，则女主拜男宾于阼阶下。子幼，则以衰抱之，人为之拜；为后者不在，则有爵者辞，无爵者人为之拜。在竟内则俟之，在竟外则殡葬可也。丧有无后，无无主。
……
en:
【Sang Da Ji (The Great Record of Mourning) No. 22】

When illness occurs, both inside and outside are swept clean. For a ruler or a high minister, the music instruments are removed; for a lower officer, the lute and zither are set aside. The dying person lies with head to the east beneath the north wall. The bed is removed. The inner garments are taken off, and new clothes are put on, with one person holding the body. Men and women change their clothes. A piece of silk floss is placed near the nose to wait for the breath to cease. A man does not die at the hands of a woman, nor a woman at the hands of a man. A ruler or his wife dies in the main hall; a high minister or his wife dies in the proper chamber; if the wife of a minister has not been formally appointed, she dies in the lower room. The body is then moved to the main hall; officers and their wives all die in the main hall.
For the calling back of the soul, if there is a forested hill, the forester sets up the ladder; if there is no forested hill, the Di people set up the ladder. The minor attendant performs the calling back, dressed in court robes. For a ruler, the robe is the dragon robe; for his wife, the qu di robe; for a high minister, the dark red robe; for his wife, the tan robe; for an officer, the jue bian cap; for an officer's wife, the shui robe. All ascend from the eastern eaves, walk on the ridge of the roof, face north and call out three times, then roll up the clothes and throw them forward. The keeper of robes receives them, and they descend from the northwestern eaves. If the deceased is a guest, the calling back is done at the public lodge, not at a private residence; if in the field, one ascends the left hub of the carriage to call back. The clothes used for calling back are not used to cover the corpse, nor for enshrouding. When calling back a woman, the skirt is not used. In all calling back, for a man the personal name is called, for a woman the courtesy name. Only weeping precedes the calling back; after the calling back, the rites of death proceed.
At the moment of death, the chief mourner wails, the brothers weep, and the women weep and leap. After the corpse is properly positioned, the son sits in the eastern position; the high ministers, great officers, fathers, elder brothers, and descendants stand in the east; the officers and minor officials weep below the hall facing north. The wife sits in the western position; the inner appointed women, aunts, sisters, and daughters stand in the west; the outer appointed women lead the outer relatives in weeping in the hall facing north. For the mourning of a high minister, the chief mourner sits in the east and the chief mourner's wife in the west; if there are appointed men and women, they sit; if not, all stand. For the mourning of an officer, the chief mourner, father, elder brothers, and descendants all sit in the east; the chief mourner's wife, aunts, sisters, and daughters all sit in the west. In all cases of weeping over the corpse in the chamber, the chief mourner holds the coverlet with both hands and weeps.
For the mourning of a ruler, before the small enshrouding, one goes out to receive visiting lords and state guests; for the mourning of a high minister, before the small enshrouding, one goes out for the ruler's command; for the mourning of an officer, one goes out for a great officer when it is not during the enshrouding. Whenever the chief mourner goes out, he is barefoot, tucks his garment into his sash, beats his breast, and descends by the western steps. The ruler bows to visiting lords and state guests in their places; for a great officer receiving the ruler's command, he meets the envoy outside the gate of the mourning hall; the envoy ascends the hall to deliver the command, and the chief mourner bows below. For an officer, when a great officer comes personally to condole, he weeps with him; he does not go out to meet him at the gate. The wife goes out for the wife of a visiting lord; the appointed woman goes out for the command of the ruler's wife; an officer's wife, when it is not during the enshrouding, goes out for an appointed woman.
For the small enshrouding, the chief mourner takes his position inside the door, and the chief mourner's wife faces east, then the enshrouding proceeds. After the enshrouding is complete, the chief mourner leans over the body and leaps, and the chief mourner's wife does the same. The chief mourner bares his arm, removes his cap, ties up his hair with hemp; the women tie up their hair with hemp and wear the hempen girdle in the chamber. The curtain is removed, and men and women carry the corpse to the hall. Then they descend to bow: the ruler bows to visiting lords and state guests; great officers and officers bow to ministers and great officers in their places, and to officers they bow three times to the side. The wife also bows to the wives of visiting lords in the hall; for great officers' wives and officers' wives, she bows to each individually; for appointed women, she bows generally to all the guests in the hall. The chief mourner returns to his position, puts on his clothes, girdle, and mourning band, and leaps. For the mourning of a mother, after taking position, the cap is removed, and then the offering is presented. Visitors to the mourning put on their fur robes, add the mourning band and girdle, and leap in turn with the chief mourner. For a ruler's mourning, the forester brings out wood and horns, the Di people bring out pots, the cook brings out a tripod, and the marshal hangs them up; then officials take turns weeping. For a high minister's mourning, officials take turns weeping without hanging pots; for an officer's mourning, weeping is done by turns without officials. In the ruler's hall, there are two torches above and two below; for a high minister, one torch above and two below; for an officer, one torch above and one below. When guests leave, the curtain is removed. Weeping over the corpse in the hall, the chief mourner is in the east; those who come from outside are in the west; the women face south. Women do not descend the hall to welcome or see off guests; if they descend, they do not weep. Men, when they go out of the mourning gate and see people, do not weep. If there is no female chief mourner, then the male chief mourner bows to female guests inside the mourning gate; if there is no male chief mourner, then the female chief mourner bows to male guests below the eastern steps. If the son is young, he is carried in mourning clothes, and others bow on his behalf. If the one who should succeed is absent, those with rank decline the bows, and those without rank have others bow for them. If he is within the borders, they wait for him; if he is outside the borders, enshrouding and burial may proceed. In mourning, there may be no heir, but there is never no chief mourner.
……

zh:
【士冠礼第一】

士冠礼。筮于庙门。主人玄冠朝服，缁带素𫖒，即位于门东，西面。有司如主人服，即位于西方，东面，北上。筮与席、所卦者，具馔于西塾。布席于门中，𫔶西阈外，西面。筮人执策，抽上韇，兼执之，进受命于主人。宰自右少退，赞命。筮人许诺，右还，即席坐，西面。卦者在左。卒筮，书卦，执以示主人。主人受视，反之。筮人还，东面，旅占，卒，进告吉。若不吉，则筮远日，如初仪。彻筮席，宗人告事毕。
主人戒宾，宾礼辞，许。主人再拜，宾答拜。主人退，宾拜送。
前期三日，筮宾，如求日之仪。
乃宿宾。宾如主人服，出门左，西面，再拜。主人东面，答拜。乃宿宾，宾许，主人再拜，宾答拜。主人退，宾拜送。宿赞冠者一人，亦如之。
厥明夕，为期于庙门之外。主人立于门东，兄弟在其南，少退，西面，北上。有司皆如宿服，立于西方，东面，北上。摈者请期，宰告曰：“质明行事。”告兄弟及有司。告事毕，摈者告期于宾之家。
夙兴，设洗，直于东荣，南北以堂深，水在洗东。陈服于房中西墉下，东领，北上。爵弁服，纁裳，纯衣，缁带，韎韐。皮弁服：素积，缁带，素韠。玄端，玄裳，黄裳、杂裳可也，缁带，爵韠。缁布冠缺项，青组缨属于缺，缁纚广终幅，长六尺，皮弁笄，爵弁笄，缁组纮，纁边，同箧。栉实于箪。蒲筵二，在南。
侧尊一甒醴，在服北。有篚，实勺、觯、角柶。脯醢，南上。爵弁、皮弁、缁布冠各一匴，执以待于西坫南，南面，东上。宾升则东面。
主人玄端爵韠，立于阼阶下，直东序，西面。兄弟毕袗玄，立于洗东，西面，北上。摈者玄端，负东塾。将冠者采衣，紒，在房中，南面。宾如主人服，赞者玄端从之，立于外门之外。
摈者告。主人迎，出门左，西面，再拜。宾答拜。
主人揖赞者，与宾揖，先入。每曲揖。至于庙门，揖入。三揖，至于阶，三让。主人升，立于序端，西面。
宾西序，东面。赞者盥于洗西，升，立于房中，西面，南上。
主人之赞者筵于东序，少北，西面。将冠者出房，南面。赞者奠纚、笄、栉于筵南端。宾揖将冠者，将冠者即筵坐。赞者坐，栉，设纚。宾降，主人降。
……
en:
[The Capping of an Ordinary Officer's Son, Part I]

The divining (with the stalks) is carried on in the doorway of the ancestral temple. The father of the boy, as Master of Ceremonies, in his dark cap, dress clothes, black silk girdle, and white knee-pads, takes his place on the east side of the doorway, with his face to the west. The assistants, dressed like the Master of Ceremonies, take their places on the west side, facing east, and graded from the north. The divining stalks, the mat, and the recording materials, are all laid out in the western gatehouse. Then the mat is spread in the doorway, to the west of the mid-post, and outside the threshold. Taking up the stalks, the diviner draws off the upper case, and holding it, along with the stalks, still in the lower case, he goes forward to take his instructions from the Master of Ceremonies. The steward, standing on the Master of Ceremonies' right, and a little behind him, assists by voicing the instructions. The diviner assents, and, turning to the right, goes to his mat and sits down, facing west, his recorder being on his left. When he has finished manipulating the stalks, the diagram resulting is written on a board, and shown to the Master of Ceremonies. He takes it, and, after looking at it, returns it. Then those taking part in the divination examine the diagram in turn, and when they have finished, the diviner reports that the result is favourable. If the result is unfavourable, they proceed to divine for a day farther off, observing the same rules as above. Then the stalks and the mat are removed. And the Director of Ceremonial announces that the business is at an end.
The Master of Ceremonies in person apprises his friends who are to be guests at the ceremony, who, after formally asking to be excused, finally consent. The Master of Ceremonies bows twice, and the guest bows in return; whereupon he withdraws, the guest bowing him farewell.
Three days before the date fixed for the ceremony they divine concerning the man selected to be the principal guest, with usages similar to those employed in divining concerning the day.
Then the Master of Ceremonies goes in person forthwith to bid the principal guest. He, dressed like the Master of Ceremonies, comes out to the left of his own door, and, turning west, bows twice. The Master of Ceremonies, facing east, returns the bows. The Master of Ceremonies then bids the guest, who accepts. The Master of Ceremonies bows twice, and the guest returns his bows. Thereafter the Master of Ceremonies retires, the guest bowing farewell to him as he goes. The bidding of the other assistants at the capping is conducted in a similar fashion.
On the eve of the day the time is fixed outside the door of the temple. The Master of Ceremonies stands to the east of the door, with his brothers and cousins to the south of him, and slightly retired, facing west, and graded from the north. The assistants, all dressed as at the bidding, stand on the west side of the door, facing east, and graded from the north. The usher asks the Master of Ceremonies to name a time; and when he has done so, the steward announces it, saying: "Tomorrow, at full light, the ceremony will commence." The usher announces this to the relatives and the assistants. The Director of Ceremonial declares that the business is at an end. Then the usher announces the time at the houses of the guests.
Rising early in the morning, they set out the used-water jar abreast the eastern wall, and as far south of it as the depth of the hall, the water being placed to the east of the jar. They then set out the clothes for the graduand under the west wall of the east chamber, collars eastwards, and graded from the north. There is the russet-coloured cap suit: the crimson skirt, the black silk coat, and the red leather knee-caps. The white deer-skin cap suit: the white surcingle, the black silk girdle, and the white knee-caps. For the suit of dark square-clothes, the dark skirt, yellow skirt, or skirt of mixed colours, black and yellow will do, with the black silk girdle and the russet knee-caps. There are also the dark cloth cap, with its band split at the back, and laced, the blue silk pin-string being fixed on to it; the black silk coif-cloth, whose breadth is the breadth of a web of cloth, and its length six feet; the hatpin worn with the skin cap, and the hatpin worn with the russet cap. The dark hat-strings are also there with their crimson edge, and all are put together in a square splint trunk. The comb is placed in a round box. Two mats are spread to the south of the clothes.
The single wine-holder is a jar of must, placed to the north of the clothes, with next it the cup-basket, in which are placed the ladle, goblet, and spoon. After this come the relishes: the dried meat, and pickled hash, graded from the south. The attendants take the russet, skin, and dark cloth caps, each in its own box, and wait to the south of the western cupboard, with their faces southward, graded from the east; and when the principal guest is ascending the steps, they face the east.
The Master of Ceremonies, in dark square clothes and russet knee-caps, stands at the foot of the eastern steps, in line with the eastern inner wall, and facing west. The relatives, in suits all black, stand behind him to the east of the water-jar, facing westward, and graded from the north. The usher, in black square-clothes, stands with his back to the east gate-house. The graduand, in coloured clothes, and with his hair tied together, stands in the chamber with his face southward. The guest, dressed like the Master of Ceremonies, and followed by his attendants in black square-clothes, stands outside the outer gate.
The usher, to whom his arrival has been intimated, announces his coming to the Master of Ceremonies. He goes to meet him, issuing by the left of the door. Turning his face west, he bows twice, the guest bowing in return.
The Master of Ceremonies then salutes the attendants, exchanges a salutation with the guest, and finally precedes him in. At each turn in their progress he again salutes. When they arrive at the door of the temple he salutes again, inviting him to enter, and in the advance up the court he salutes three times. When they arrive at the steps they mutually yield precedence three times. Then the Master of Ceremonies ascends, and stands at the end of the eastern inner wall, facing west;
and the guest, standing at the end of the west inner wall, faces east. The attendants wash their hands at the west side of the used-water jar, and then go up, and stand within the chamber, facing west, and graded from the south.
The assistant to the Master of Ceremonies spreads a mat near the end of the east inner wall, a little to the north, and facing west. The graduand issues from the chamber, and stands with his face to the south. The assistant lays out the coif-cloth, hatpin, and comb on the southern end of the mat. The principal guest salutes the graduand, who goes forward to the mat and sits down; after which the assistant combs his hair, and puts on him the coif-cloth. The guest goes down the western steps to wash his hands, while the Master of Ceremonies goes down those on the east, the guest declining the honour, and the Master of Ceremonies making a suitable reply.

这世上人会变，心会变，但包子、饼和油馍不会变。
他的不着调哥哥也没有变，依旧闹事，依旧不着四六，依旧日日挨打。
en:
He's been running his steamed bun stall here for eight years, quietly watching people come and go. Some stop by today, others tomorrow, and some just don't come back. 
The young customer who, two years ago, boasted about making a name for himself in Kaifeng City had now returned—quiet, worn out, and dressed in rags. 
Another regular customer who, three years ago, used to rave about his amazing Scallion Pancakes had now strolled through town dressed in silk, bragging about the fancy food in Kaifeng's restaurants. 
People change. So do their hearts. But steamed buns, pancakes, and fried dough? They stay the same. 
And his reckless brother? He hasn't changed a bit—still causing trouble all over the place and getting into fights every day.
So that's why...

The soldiers at the Toilgrain Barn rescued two cats and two dogs. Ever since they gathered, they've been arguing incessantly, each believing they've done the most for the camp.
Acrobat has a skill that no other cat or dog possesses. He can perform acrobatics.
During the day, while the soldiers are hard at work transporting grain, Acrobat leaps between the tents. Whenever the soldiers look up, they see him diligently doing somersaults.
At night, when the bonfires are lit and soldiers and commoners gather together, Acrobat appears by their side. With a kick of his hind legs and a powerful leap, he clears the fire and curls up obediently in someone's arms.
Wherever Acrobat is, there is endless laughter and joy.

淮深亲启：
东频来信，催我启程。此去后，河西与破白，都托予你。
自兄长东去，你父子二人再不得见，是我之过。如今我也要去往长安，你若有话，便让我一并带去吧。
这些日子，书房门都被你踹坏了，日日同我议事至鸡鸣。此后你不必问谁，也不用管我下过的命令，自行决定。归义二字，只需对得起天地，便皆可为。
我走后，若有信寄来，署名张议潮，统统别看，丢到炉子里烧了取暖就是。
你记好，从此往后，河西没有大张将军，只有小张将军。拿好破白，你且去！
en:
For Huaishen's eyes only:

The court hounds me with letters, demanding my journey east. After my departure, Hexi and the Dawnfang are yours to command.

Since your father's departure, you two have never seen each other again. That is my fault. Now I follow his path to Chang'an. If you have a message, I will be its bearer.

You've spent these nights practically living in my study, arguing with me till dawn. From now on, you'll have no one to argue with. You need not ask for permission, and you need not follow my old commands. Do what you see fit. So long as your actions are worthy of the name Guiyi, nothing is forbidden.

Once I am gone, if any letter comes for Zhang Yichao, pay it no mind. Use it for kindling.

Remember this: Hexi no longer has a Great General Zhang. It has only a Little General Zhang. Take the Dawnfang, and forge your own path!

一猫一鼠，跑起来就发疯了，忘情了，没命了！
草丛里划出风一般的痕迹，猫尾巴欢快地竖着，高高的。

en:
When she was small, Persimmon loved to play a game.
Whatever rustled in the tall grass, she'd bet herself what it was. A mouse? A bird?
Paws sweating, she'd peer through the blades.
If she was right, dinner was a little mouse!
She'd burst out with a mighty "Mrow!" and the little creature would squeak and drop whatever it was carrying, a nut, a berry, a stolen scrap, and flee for its life.
They'd tear through the meadow like the wind, her tail a happy, upright flag.
Win or lose, the night held a prize: fresh meat or a sweet, stolen persimmon.

zh: 豫章故郡，洪都新府。星分翼轸，地接衡庐。襟三江而带五湖，控蛮荆而引瓯越。物华天宝，龙光射牛斗之墟；人杰地灵，徐孺下陈蕃之榻。雄州雾列，俊采星驰。台隍枕夷夏之交，宾主尽东南之美。都督阎公之雅望，棨戟遥临；宇文新州之懿范，襜帷暂驻。十旬休假，胜友如云；千里逢迎，高朋满座。腾蛟起凤，孟学士之词宗；紫电青霜，王将军之武库。家君作宰，路出名区；童子何知，躬逢胜饯。
en: Yuzhang, the ancient prefecture, is now the new capital of Hongdu. The stars are divided into wings and chariots, the land connects Heng and Lu. It is surrounded by the three rivers and five lakes, controlling the southern barbarians and guiding the Ouyue. The land is rich in resources, with the dragon's light shining over the ruins of the Ox and Dipper. The place is blessed with talented people, where Xu Ru once sat by Chen Fan's couch. The magnificent state is enveloped in mist, and the brilliant talents are like stars rushing across the sky. The platform and city sit at the intersection of the barbarian and the civilized, with both the host and guest embodying the beauty of the Southeast. Governor Yan's esteemed reputation reaches far, with his scepter far away; the noble example of Yu Wen of Xinzhu, temporarily staying under a simple canopy. On a ten-day holiday, I am surrounded by excellent friends like clouds; with a thousand-mile greeting, my place is filled with high-profile guests. The dragon rises, the phoenix ascends, the words of Scholar Meng set the standard; purple lightning and blue frost are the weapons of General Wang's armory. My father serves as the governor, and the road leads to a famous district; what does a young boy know? He is fortunate to attend a grand farewell feast.

zh:
沈玉的院子太小，每日只能靠着院外飞来的几只鸟解闷，误入之人比平日的鸟雀热闹有趣许多。
于是她随手撒了一把鸟食，算是谢他今晚来过。

但她却发现自己摆明了被赖上了。
沈玉听说过有人喂了路边的野猫，那猫便好几日在家门口徘徊不去，可这只鸟分明不是无处可去的鸟，他皮毛光鲜，分明是被人娇养，瞧上去没什么心眼，想来也并未在外摸爬滚打过几次，为何要在这里日日徘徊。
像是谢她，日日夜里，他便从外头衔来故事。

沈玉是喜欢听故事的。
这方寸庭院太小，只能瞧见一片天；每一本书，都写着无般一二的话，爹选定了，说一声好，让人摆在她的书柜之中；每一餐吃食，多了少了都不可；每一日的时辰，都规规矩矩地待在被另一个人钉好的架子里。
旁人的日子是一本书，一页一页大不相同，今日有今日的新鲜，明日有明日的快活，她的日子是一页纸，翻来覆去都是一样的字，于是一日一日，她只能翻着那张纸，直到把日子揉得泛皱，把书页瞧得泛黄。
他是她的另一页纸，是她的第二个故事。

他像是一只从笼子里飞出来的鸟，但在沈玉明白，她身上的笼子比他重上许多，他在藤条编织的笼子里，而她的身上是沉甸甸的金银锁链，他还可以勉强振动翅膀，她却连表情都无法自己雕刻，她如何能留下这个故事。

沈玉的书房里，层层叠叠压着厚厚的纸张，她的岁月里，循环往复着一张书页，但是再厚重的纸张和书页，只需要一点火星，便可焚烧殆尽，但烧了，又有什么用呢。
烧了这一处，还有那一处，烧了这间屋子，还有那间屋子，砍了一条锁链，还有无数条锁链。
她不再看了，闭上眼，喂喂鸟，听话，或者假装听话。
en:
Shen Yu's courtyard was too small, her only amusement the few birds that flitted over the walls each day. But the man who strayed in that night was livelier than any sparrow.
She tossed him a handful of birdseed as thanks for the evening's distraction.

Yet she soon realized she'd been claimed.
She'd heard of people feeding stray cats, only to have them linger for days. But this "bird" was no stray. His fine plumage spoke of pampering, his guileless eyes of sheltered inexperience. Why, then, did he keep returning?
As thanks, he brought her stories every night, carried in on his tongue like nesting materials.

Shen Yu loved stories.
Her tiny courtyard offered only a sliver of sky. Every book in her collection held the same tedious virtues, handpicked by her father and neatly shelved. Every meal was measured, every hour dictated by a rigid schedule.
Others live their lives like books, each page splashed with new colors, today's surprises bleeding into tomorrow's joys. But hers was a single sheet, the same characters pressed over and over, until the paper grew soft with handling, the ink fading to a tired yellow.
He was her new page, her second story.

He seemed a bird escaped from a wicker cage, but Shen Yu knew her own cage was heavier. His was woven of rattan, hers, of gilded chains. He could still flutter his wings. She couldn't even control her expressions. How could she keep this story?

In her study, stacks of paper pressed down on her years, each day a tedious reprint of the last. But even the thickest manuscripts could burn with a single spark. What good would ashes do?
Burn this room, and another cage will remain. Sever one chain, and a hundred more would bind her.
She closed her eyes. Better to feed her bird, to pretend to obey.

zh:
开元中，上元夜，玄宗于上阳宫张华灯为山，缀绮罗千树，自殿阁至宫门，光彻如昼。
时有方士叶法善侍侧，奏曰：“今夕灯事之盛，寰宇莫京，然凉州稍可拟耳。”
帝异之，曰：“卿素游凉州耶？”对曰：“适自彼境，闻敕即至。”上愈奇，曰：“朕欲一游凉州，可乎？”
法善请帝暝目凝息，但觉风雷激荡于襟袖间。
少顷足履实地，视之，果见千灯竞辉，香尘漫野，红楼连亘如昼，清夜荧煌若春。凉州胜景，尽在樽俎须臾矣。
en:
On the Lantern Festival night of the Kaiyuan era, Emperor Xuanzong hung elaborate lanterns in Shangyang Palace, piling them like mountains and adorning with silk brocades as dense as blooming trees. From palaces to palace gates, the light shone as bright as day. 
At that time, the Taoist master Ye Fashan stood by and said, "Tonight's lantern festival is unmatched under heaven, only Liangzhou's comes close." 
The emperor was surprised, "Have you ever traveled to Liangzhou?" He replied, "I just came from there and hurried here at your call." The emperor was even more amazed, "I wish to visit Liangzhou, can we go?" 
Ye Fashan told him to close his eyes and hold his breath. At once, the emperor felt wind and thunder surging around his robes. 
In a moment, he touched solid ground. Opening his eyes, he saw thousands of lanterns glowing, fragrant dust covering the fields, red mansions stretching like daylight, and the quiet night shining warm as spring. Liangzhou's scenery unfolded before him in an instant.

zh:
凉州有美酒，谓之葡萄；凉州有明月，可取月华。相传，有佳酿月光酒，取葡萄精魄，融月华而成。饮者或言可睹故园烟景，然终是传闻。  
玉露台畔，曾有一方葡萄园，居者一家三人。晨起剪枝，暮至压榨，指节皆染碧紫。彼等深信掌中老茧可酿甘醴，瓮中浊浆能易安乐。
可葡萄滴翠甜美，可曾尝见人世甘苦？月轮几度满亏，岂能照亮命途褶皱？家人离散，只留稚女独守荒园。有人曾见她抱月而哭泣，或陶碗盛月，饮之则泪落如珠。
en:
In Liangzhou, a famed grape wine is infused with the moon's essence to create the rare "Moonlight Wine," said to grant drinkers fleeting visions of their distant homeland.   
Beside the Jade Dew Terrace, there once was a small vineyard where a family of three lived. They pruned vines at dawn and pressed grapes at dusk, their knuckles stained deep purple. They firmly believed the calluses on their palms could brew sweet nectar, and the turbid juice in their jars could be exchanged for peace and happiness. 
But can the emerald sweetness of grapes ever taste the bitterness of human life? How many waxings and wanings of the moon could ever illuminate the wrinkles of fate? The family scattered, leaving only a young girl to guard the desolate garden alone. Some have seen her embracing the moon and weeping, or holding the moon in a clay bowl, drinking it down with tears falling like pearls.

zh: “石敢当”之名最早见于西汉史游所编的儿童启蒙识字书。 唐代学者颜师古对此注解道：“敢当，所向无敌也。”唐代将石敢当与石刻联系，将其视为镇宅辟邪的祥物。至宋时，随着随着泰山崇拜的盛行，民间为了赋予石敢当更强的神力，将其与作为“五岳之尊”和“幽冥主宰”的泰山信仰相融合，出现了“泰山石敢当”。
en:
The name Shigandang (literally "one who dares resist all") first appeared in a children's literacy primer compiled by Shi You during the Western Han dynasty. Tang dynasty scholar Yan Shigu later explained the phrase as meaning "invincible in the face of all threats." Over time, the concept evolved into physical warding stones inscribed with the name and placed near homes to repel evil spirits.
By the Song dynasty, as Mount Tai worship grew in popularity, people merged these protective markers with beliefs surrounding Mount Tai, revered as the foremost of the Five Sacred Peaks and a ruler of the underworld. In doing so, they endowed it with even greater spiritual power, giving rise to the form known as "Mount Tai Warding Stones" (Taishan Shigandang).

zh:
今儿晌午，我正走得口干舌燥，眼前豁然出现一片桃林！圆滚滚的桃子挂满了枝头，别提多喜人了。
我隔老远就闻到了甜丝丝的香味，于是三步并作两步，忙蹿了过去，伸手摘得一个……老天，当真是及时雨啊！
我刚在阴凉的地方坐稳当，准备享用这果子呢，就瞧见不远处走来两个彪形大汉！他们腰里别着家伙，一看就不是善茬儿。我赶紧把桃子往怀里一揣，缩在树后，大气都不敢喘……
这二人骂骂咧咧的，我倒听了个七七八八……原来他们是附近山寨的恶匪，他们大当家的不知跑哪儿去了，二当家的又不成事，可半路忽冒出个什么狄爷，压得他们不敢作乱。听口气，这匪窝里头也不太平呢。
那两人嘟嘟囔囔走远了，我才觉着后背凉飕飕的，衣裳都贴肉上了！我也不敢多留，手忙脚乱又摘了几个桃子，便猫着腰溜了出去。
好家伙，真是险之又险！桃是好桃，脆甜得很，可这地方……我说什么都不会再来了！
唉，这桃子，我还是走远些再吃罢。
en:
This noon, I was walking along, parched and weary, when suddenly a peach grove appeared before my eyes! Round, plump peaches hung heavy on every branch... A joyful sight!
I caught a sweet fragrance from far off, so I hurried over in quick strides and picked one... Heavens, what a timely blessing!
I'd just settled down in the shade to enjoy the fruit when I saw two hulking men approaching! Weapons at their waists, clearly up to no good. I quickly stuffed the peach into my robe and shrank behind a tree, not daring to breathe...
They cursed and grumbled, and I caught most of what they said... Turns out they're villains from a nearby mountain stronghold. Their chief has vanished somewhere, and the second-in-command is useless, but some fellow calling himself Master Di suddenly showed up and kept them from causing trouble. From the sound of it, even that den of thieves isn't at peace.
They wandered off, muttering, and only then did I feel the chill on my back... my clothes were soaked through with sweat! I didn't dare linger, so I fumbled and grabbed a few more peaches before slipping away, hunched low.
Whew, that was close! The peaches were good, crisp and sweet, but that place... I swear I'll never go back!
Alas, I suppose I'll wait until I'm farther away before eating this peach.

The horse lifts its head and neighs, with three hooves in the air and its right hind hoof poised on the back of a flying swallow. The bird twists its head in surprise, emphasizing the horse's astonishing speed. Heaps of rice fill the threshing ground, carts brim with grain. Every home rings with chickens and dogs, and mulberries decorate the fields. 

Dog breeding was quite popular during the Song Dynasty. Breeds like the Yulin dog and the Luojiang dog were especially beloved by the people. Among the general populace, a body of canine-related knowledge even emerged. One curious example was "dog dream omens," which interpreted human dreams involving dogs and reflected Song-era beliefs about dreams. The Menglin Xuanjie records: "To be bitten on the head by a dog in the marketplace is auspicious." This means that dreaming of being bitten on the head by a dog in a market signifies a great fortune, such as achieving top honors in the imperial exams.

zh: 茶百戏，又称“水丹青”、“分茶”，是一种能使茶汤纹脉形成物象的民间艺术，特点是仅用茶和水不用其他的原料能在茶汤中显现出文字和图像。碾茶为末，注之以汤，以筅击拂。由于茶汤显现的纹理丰富、自然、灵动，此时盏面上的汤纹水脉会幻变出种种图样，若山水云雾，状花鸟虫鱼，恰如一幅幅水墨图画。
en: Often called "water painting" or "tea division," this is a remarkable traditional art form where intricate images and words are drawn onto the surface of a cup of tea using no pigments other than tea and water. The resulting foam is so rich and fluid that a skilled artisan can manipulate it to form swirling patterns of misty mountains, flowers, and birds, making it look exactly like a delicate ink-wash painting.

zh:
洛鲤河鲂，贵于牛羊。

唐代孔颖达《毛诗注疏》引陆机曰：鲂，今伊洛济颖鲂鱼也。广而薄肥，恬而少力，细鳞，鱼之美者。说的便是这洛河水中的鲂鱼，这里的鲂鱼就是今天的鳊鱼，这种鱼腹中多脂肪，十分肥美，在古代是餐桌上难得的奢侈品。诗经中也曾说道，岂其食鱼，必河之鲂？岂其取妻，必齐之姜。将美人与鲂鱼相提并论，可见其在古人眼中的尊崇地位，怪不得有谚语说，洛鲤河鲂，贵于牛羊呢！
en:
Luo's carp and bream, worth more than livestock. 

Tang Dynasty scholar Kong Yingda cited Lu Ji in his Mao Poetry Commentary: "The bream—now found in the Yiluo, Ji, and Ying rivers—are broad, thin, fatty, mild-tempered, with fine scales, the finest of fish." This refers to the black bream of the Luo River, known today as bian fish. Rich in belly fat, they were a rare delicacy on ancient tables. As The Book of Songs mused: "Must one eat only Luo's bream? Must one marry only Qi's daughters?" Comparing women of beauty to fine fish shows how revered black bream was, and thus the saying: "Luo's carp and bream, worth more than livestock."

愚弟听闻玉门关处有一奇所，这百十年间，河西武林人士去之恐有千余却无一人能回。
至于这奇所奇在何处，有谣传称，其内一日胜似世间数十年。
有人言，内有金银财宝，有人言，内有盖世神功，更有人言，内有美人无数。
总之，是个天下第一好去处，否则武林中高手者众，怎会有千余人去竟无一人能回？

en:
For My Brother Guo's Eyes Alone,

Rumor reaches me of a strange place near Jade Gate Pass. For more than a century, warriors from all across Hexi have gone there—perhaps a thousand in number—and not a single one has ever returned.

What makes the place so extraordinary? Tales differ wildly. Some say a single day within equals decades in the outside world.
Others claim it holds unmatched martial arts, while still more whisper of gold, jewels, and countless beauties.

Whatever the truth, it is hailed as the finest place under heaven. Why else would so many masters go, never to come back?
Perhaps it is a Haven beyond the mortal world, a place so wondrous one forgets to leave.

I intend to see for myself. If this tale stirs your heart as it does mine, meet me at the spot marked on the map.

Respectfully, your humble younger brother, Bai Ying

zh:
【定公第十一】

元年，春，王。
不言正月，定无正也。定之无正何也？昭公之终，非正终也。定之始，非正始也。昭无正终，故定无正始。不言即位，丧在外也。
○三月，晋人执宋仲几于京师。
此其大夫，其曰人何也？微之也。何为微之？不正其执人于尊者之所也，不与大夫之伯讨也。
○夏，六月，癸亥，公之丧至自干侯。
○戊辰，公即位。
殡，然后即位也。定无正，见无以正也。踰年不言即位，是有故公也。言即位，是无故公也。即位，授受之道也。先君无正终，则后君无正始也；先君有正终，则后君有正始也。戊辰，公即位，谨之也。定之即位，不可不察也。公即位，何以日也？戊辰之日，然后即位也。癸亥，公之丧至自干侯，何为戊辰之日然后即位也？正君乎国，然后即位也。沈子曰:"正棺乎两楹之间，然后即位也。"内之大事日，即位，君之大事也，其不日何也？以年决者，不以日决也。此则其日何也？着之也。何着焉？踰年即位，厉也，于厉之中，又有义焉。未殡，虽有天子之命犹不敢，况临诸臣乎？周人有丧，鲁人有丧，周人吊，鲁人不吊。周人曰:"固吾臣也，使人可也。"鲁人曰:"吾君也，亲之者也，使大夫则不可也。"故周人吊，鲁人不吊，以其下成康为未久也。君至尊也，去父之殡而往吊，犹不敢，况未殡而临诸臣乎？
○秋，七月，癸巳，葬我君昭公。
○九月，大雩。
雩月，雩之正也。秋大雩，非正也。冬大雩，非正也。秋大雩，雩之为非正何也？毛泽未尽，人力未竭，未可以雩也。雩月，雩之正也，月之为雩之正何也？其时穷，人力尽，然后雩，雩之正也。何谓其时穷人力尽？是月不雨，则无及矣。是年不艾，则无食矣，是谓其时穷，人力尽也。雩之必待其时穷人力尽何也？雩者，为旱求者也。求者，请也，古之人重请。何重乎请？人之所以为人也，让也。请道去让也，则是舍其所以为人也，是以重之。焉请哉？请乎应上公。古之神人有应上公者，通乎阴阳。君亲帅诸大夫道之而以请焉。夫请者，非可诒托而往也，必亲之者也，是以重之。
○立炀宫。
立者，不宜立者也。
○冬，十月，陨霜杀菽。
未可以杀而杀，举重。可杀而不杀，举轻。其曰菽，举重也。

二年，春，王正月。
○夏，五月，壬辰，雉门及两观灾。
其不曰雉门灾及两观何也？灾自两观始也，不以尊者亲灾也。先言雉门，尊尊也。
○秋，楚人伐吴。
○冬，十月，新作雉门及两观。
言新，有旧也。作，为也，有加度也，此不正。其以尊者亲之何也？虽不正也，于美犹可也。

……
en:
【Duke Ding, Year 11】

First year, spring, the King.
It does not say "first month," because Ding had no proper beginning. Why did Ding have no proper beginning? Duke Zhao's end was not a proper end. Ding's beginning was not a proper beginning. Since Zhao had no proper end, Ding had no proper beginning. It does not say "ascended the throne," because the mourning was still abroad.
○ In the third month, the people of Jin seized Zhong Ji of Song in the capital.
He was their high officer, yet it says "people"—why? To belittle them. Why belittle them? Because it was improper to seize someone in the place of the Exalted, and they did not approve of a high officer undertaking a punitive expedition.
○ In summer, in the sixth month, on the day Guihai, the Duke's coffin arrived from Ganhou.
○ On the day Wuchen, the Duke ascended the throne.
Only after the encoffining did he ascend the throne. Ding had no proper beginning, showing there was nothing by which to establish propriety. When one does not announce accession after the year has passed, it is because there was a former ruler with cause. When one announces accession, it is because there was no former ruler with cause. Accession is the way of handing over and receiving. If the former ruler had no proper end, then the later ruler had no proper beginning; if the former ruler had a proper end, then the later ruler had a proper beginning. On Wuchen, the Duke ascended the throne—this is a matter of caution. Ding's accession cannot but be examined. Why is the day recorded for the Duke's accession? Because it was on the day Wuchen that he then ascended the throne. On Guihai, the Duke's coffin arrived from Ganhou—why did he ascend the throne only on the day Wuchen? Because he rectified his rule over the state, and only then ascended the throne. Master Shen said: "After the coffin is properly placed between the two pillars, then one ascends the throne." Major events within the state are dated; accession is a major event of the ruler—why is it not dated here? Because it is determined by the year, not by the day. Why then is it dated here? To make it prominent. What is made prominent? Ascending the throne after the year has passed is a crisis, and within the crisis there is also righteousness. Before the encoffining, even if there were a mandate from the Son of Heaven, one would still not dare—how much less when facing the assembled ministers? When the Zhou people had a mourning, and the Lu people had a mourning, the Zhou people sent condolences, but the Lu people did not. The Zhou people said: "They are surely our subjects; sending a messenger is acceptable." The Lu people said: "He is our ruler, one to be mourned personally; sending a high officer would not be acceptable." Therefore the Zhou people sent condolences, but the Lu people did not, because the time since Cheng and Kang was not yet distant. The ruler is most exalted; to leave one's father's bier and go to offer condolences, one still would not dare—how much less, before the encoffining, to face the assembled ministers?
○ In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Guisi, we buried our ruler, Duke Zhao.
○ In the ninth month, the Great Rain Prayer.
When the rain prayer is dated by month, it is proper. The Great Rain Prayer in autumn is improper. The Great Rain Prayer in winter is improper. Why is the Great Rain Prayer in autumn improper? Because the moisture of the crops was not yet exhausted, and the strength of the people was not yet spent; it was not yet time for the rain prayer. When the rain prayer is dated by month, it is proper—why is dating it by month proper? Because when the season is exhausted and the people's strength is spent, then one prays for rain—that is proper. What does "the season is exhausted and the people's strength is spent" mean? If in this month there is no rain, then there will be nothing to rely on. If in this year there is no harvest, then there will be no food. This is called the season being exhausted and the people's strength spent. Why must the rain prayer wait until the season is exhausted and the people's strength is spent? The rain prayer is a request made for drought. A request is a plea. The ancients took pleas seriously. Why did they take pleas seriously? What makes a person a person is deference. The way of pleading sets aside deference, and thus it abandons what makes one a person—therefore they took it seriously. Where did they plead? They pleaded to the High Responder. Among the ancient spirit-men was the High Responder, who communicated with yin and yang. The ruler personally led the high officers to guide the way and plead. Such a plea was not something that could be delegated or entrusted to another; it had to be done personally—therefore it was taken seriously.
○ The Yang Palace was established.
"Established" means it should not have been established.
○ In winter, in the tenth month, frost fell and killed the beans.
When it kills what should not yet be killed, the greater harm is noted. When it could kill but does not, the lesser harm is noted. Saying "beans" notes the greater harm.

Second year, spring, the King's first month.
○ In summer, in the fifth month, on the day Renchen, the Pheasant Gate and the two towers caught fire.
Why does it not say "the Pheasant Gate caught fire and then the two towers"? Because the fire started from the two towers, and one does not attribute disaster to the more honored. Mentioning the Pheasant Gate first honors the honored.
○ In autumn, the people of Chu attacked Wu.
○ In winter, in the tenth month, the Pheasant Gate and the two towers were newly built.
Saying "newly" indicates there was something old. "Built" means made, with added scale—this was improper. Why is it attributed to the honored? Although improper, in terms of beauty it was still acceptable.

自慈心镇出北门，过石溪，行十里，路有歧，东向璧泉山，又三十里，抵千佛谷。此处本为璧泉山脚无名峡谷，因多产坚石，慈心镇匠人常采石以成佛雕，更有百余佛雕师为表虔诚，于谷间雕佛万千，或立或卧，形态各异，不一而足，高者百尺有余，颇具宝相庄严，技艺实属难得。
然千佛盛景未成乃止，盖因前朝显德年间，世宗禁绝佛教。自废以来，石刻尤存，信仰不再，千佛亦无人问津久矣。
en:
From Mercyheart Town go through the north gate, crossing the rocky creek, and travel ten miles, where the path forks. Heading east toward Jadebrook Mountain, after another thirty miles, one arrives at Thousand-Buddha Vale.
Originally an unnamed gorge at the foot of Jadebrook Mountain, it abounded in hard stone—thus craftsmen from Mercyheart Town often quarried here to carve Buddha statues. What's more, over a hundred Buddha sculptors, to show their piety, sculpted thousands of Buddhas in the valley: standing or reclining, in all manner of postures. The tallest exceed a hundred feet, exuding majestic dignity—a truly remarkable feat of craftsmanship.
Yet the grandeur of Thousand Buddhas was never completed, for during the Xiande era of the previous dynasty, Emperor Shizong suppressed Buddhism. Since the suppression, the stone carvings remain, but faith has faded, and the thousand Buddhas have been neglected for ages.

zh:
游侠亲启：
流年易老，山河依旧。近日我四处寻幽览胜，收集七夕节俗，见到不少有意思的事情。
有些地方要在太阳底下曝衣晒书，有些地方要在月下穿针乞巧。就连吃巧果的风俗也各不相同，有偏好原味入口的、有只吃芝麻煎炸的。还有些地方特地存着不吃，风干成串，挂在孩子身上祈福，说是可以一直留到过年。
一不小心买来太多，我自己吃不完，便想起你来。和清河常吃的味道不太一样，香甜微咸各拿了些，你都尝尝。
en:
Dear Wanderer,
Time flies, yet the world remains. I've been traveling off the beaten path lately, taking in the sights and seeing how different towns celebrate Qixi Festival, and I've stumbled upon some really interesting customs.
In some places, they air out their clothes and books in the sun, while in others, they thread needles under the moonlight to pray for a deft hand. Even the way people eat Skill Fruits varies: some prefer them plain, while others only eat them deep-fried in sesame. Some places don't eat them at all. They air-dry these fruits, string them into necklaces, and hang them on kids for good luck, claiming they'll keep right up until the New Year.
I accidentally bought way too many to finish on my own, and naturally, I thought of you. The flavors are a bit different from what we usually have back in Qinghe. I packed a mix of sweet and slightly savory ones. I hope you enjoy them.

zh:
薛丑对父亲最后的印象，是他离去时的背影，而这背影如今也模糊不清了。那个粟特商人给了他一半的血肉，却也仅限于此。
他只些许记得，他曾伸出手，想抓住父亲身上垂落的衣带，但他失败了，衣带从他手中滑落——和所有他想抓住的东西一样。
这一年，薛丑六岁，中原连年战乱，那个粟特商人终于不再心存侥幸，抛下孤儿寡母独自回国，离开了曾经幻想过的“大唐盛世”。从这个角度来说，他的确是个货真价实的商人。

天灾人祸的荒年里，薛丑和娘亲相依为命。当然，这是薛丑自己以为的。因为他的娘亲为了活命，和另一个流民约定易子而食。很多年后，薛丑才明白，那一刻他体会到的感觉名为“背叛”。可那时的他，有什么资格这样想呢？
分别前，薛丑静静地看着她，直到，在她的眼眸里看到一滴掉落的泪。薛丑想，这就够了，这就够了。你会活下来的，我也会。只是从此陌路，相见不识。这一去，就算还了她的生养之恩。

沸水在破旧的铁锅里发出愉悦的咕嘟声，薛丑发力踢翻了烧水的破锅，沸水溅到那人身上，烫得对方发狂。薛丑转身向屋外跑去，可他还是太弱小了，那人抓住了他。挣扎间，他的左脸被按在滚烫的锅底，留下一片难看的疤痕。
“疤痕？那……”
“嗤，不然呢，老子活得好好的，你以为跟你说话的是鬼吗？”
“啧，太难看了……我也是要脸的好吧。”

许是命不该绝，薛丑的叫声引起了过路的朱佑生的注意，他被救下了。看着面前英姿飒爽的少年侠客，薛丑眼珠一转，可怜兮兮地说自己是个孤儿，无处可去。薛丑觉得自己说得是大实话，才没有说谎。
于是，朱佑生带着他找到鬼市子的幻术师薛老儿。从此，他有了新的名字，薛丑。
跟着师父前往瓦子的那天，薛丑很认真地对朱佑生说：“将来你继任道主，我会回来帮你。”朱佑生大笑着应好，并没有将少年的话当真。可薛丑当真了，他很认真。
en:
Xue Chou's last memory of his father is the man's retreating figure, now faded and indistinct in his mind. The Sogdian merchant had given Xue Chou half his blood, but nothing more.
He only vaguely recalls reaching out to grab the sash hanging from his father's robe, but failing as it slipped through his fingers, just like everything else he'd tried to hold onto.
That year, Xue Chou was six. With constant wars plaguing the Central Plains, the Sogdian merchant finally abandoned hope, deserting his wife and child to return home, leaving behind the "Great Tang prosperity" he had once fantasized about. In that sense, he was every bit the merchant.

Through lean years of natural disaster and social upheaval, Xue Chou clung to his mother. Or so he thought. For she had struck a deal with another refugee: to eat each other's children to survive. It would take years for Xue Chou to name that feeling in his chest: betrayal. But what right did he have to feel that way back then?Before parting, Xue Chou stared at her in silence until he saw a tear fall from her eye. This is enough, he thought. This is enough. You will live, and so will I. But from now on, we are strangers who pass without recognition. This farewell would repay her for giving him life.

The boiling water gurgled merrily in the rusted iron pot. Xue Chou kicked it over, scalding the refugee's skin and triggering a mad scramble. He turned to flee, but he was too weak. The man grabbed him. In the struggle, his left cheek was pressed against the searing pot bottom, leaving a grotesque scar."A scar? But..."
"Snort. What, did you think I was a ghost? I'm very much alive."
"Ugh, it's hideous... I care about my appearance, you know."

By some stroke of luck, Xue Chou's cries drew the attention of Zhu Yousheng, a passing swordsman. After being rescued, Xue Chou looked up at the dashing young hero, then lied glibly about being an orphan with nowhere to go. At least, he told himself it wasn't a lie, just omitting the truth.
Zhu Yousheng took him to Xue Lao'er, an illusionist in Ghostlight Market. Thus, he gained a new name: Xue Chou.
The day he followed his master to the Entertainment District, Xue Chou turned to Zhu Yousheng and said earnestly, "When you become the Dao Lord, I will return to help you." Zhu Yousheng laughed and agreed, not taking the boy's words seriously. But Xue Chou did. He always did.

zh:
“孩儿勿虑……我和你娘，没什么仇家……”
那年，伊刀十岁上下。他和兄长守着血泊中的双亲，嘴唇颤抖却都说不出话。
“我们为昔日承诺，心甘自刎。老大、老二，你们要……好好活。记住……人活一世，决不可无信……”

那一日，跟随伊刀父母一起下葬的，还有他对这世道的疑惑。
“大哥……爹娘就这么没了？凭什么……！”年幼的伊刀，声音中听不到一丝哭腔，但脸上的泪却挂不住。
哥哥拍了拍他的肩膀，“凭什么？我也不知道。他们因信而死，你我要守信而活……”
“这是……爹娘最后留下的嘱托了……”伊刀看着他世上最后的亲人，擦干了脸上的泪痕。
“甭管什么世道，后面的血路，咱哥俩一起闯了。”
“嗯，大哥！”
伊刀不再问凭什么、问为什么，他心中只烙下了“人活一世，决不可无信”这几个字。
 
至于其他的？仁义礼智，皆是扯淡。
en:
"Don't fret, son... Your mother and I... we have no enemies..." That year, Yi Dao was barely ten. Kneeling beside his dying parents in a pool of blood, he and his elder brother trembled, wordless.
"We took our own lives willingly for an old promise. Sons... live well. Remember... in life, never break your word..."

Buried with his parents that day was Yi Dao's faith in the world's justice.
"Brother... are Mother and Father really gone? How can this be...?" The young Yi Dao's voice held no sobs, but tears streamed down his face.
His brother gripped his shoulder. "Why? I don't know. They died for their word. We'll live by ours."
"This... is their last lesson." Yi Dao stared at his only remaining kin, wiping his face.
"No matter how cruel the world is, we'll forge through the bloodshed together, brother."
"Yes, brother!"
Yi Dao never again asked "how" or "why." The only thing seared into his heart was: In life, never break your word.

As for the rest—benevolence, righteousness, ritual, wisdom? All empty lies.

【万章章句上】

万章问曰：舜往于田，号泣于旻天，何为其号泣也？孟子曰：怨慕也。
万章曰：父母爱之，喜而不忘；父母恶之，劳而不怨。然则舜怨乎？
曰：长息问于公明高曰：舜往于田，则吾既得闻命矣；号泣于旻天，于父母，则吾不知也。公明高曰：是非尔所知也。夫公明高以孝子之心为不若是恝，我竭力耕田，共为子职而已矣。父母之不我爱，于我何哉？帝使其子九男二女，百官牛羊仓廪备，以事舜于畎亩之中。天下之士多就之者。帝将胥天下而迁之焉。为不顺于父母，如穷人无所归。天下之士悦之，人之所欲也，而不足以解忧；好色，人之所欲，妻帝之二女，而不足以解忧；富，人之所欲，富有天下，而不足以解忧；贵，人之所欲，贵为天子，而不足以解忧。人悦之、好色、富、贵，无足以解忧者，惟顺于父母，可以解忧。人少则慕父母；知好色则慕少艾；有妻子则慕妻子；仕则慕君，不得于君则热中。大孝，终身慕父母。五十而慕者，予于大舜见之矣。
万章问曰：诗云：娶妻如之何？必告父母。信斯言也，宜莫如舜。舜之不告而娶，何也？
孟子曰：告则不得娶。男女居室，人之大伦也。如告，则废人之大伦，以怼父母，是以不告也。
万章曰：舜之不告而娶，则吾既得闻命矣。帝之妻舜而不告，何也？
曰：帝亦知告焉则不得妻也。
万章曰：父母使舜完廪，捐阶，瞽瞍焚廪，使浚井，出，从而掩之。象曰：谟盖都君，咸我绩。牛羊，父母；仓廪，父母。干戈，朕；琴，朕；弤，朕；二嫂，使治朕栖。象往入舜宫，舜在床琴。象曰：郁陶思君尔。忸怩。舜曰：惟兹臣庶，汝其于予治。不识舜不知象之将杀己与？
曰：奚而不知也？象忧亦忧，象喜亦喜。
曰：然则舜伪喜者与？
曰：否。昔者有馈生鱼于郑子产，子产使校人畜之池。校人烹之，反命曰：始舍之，圉圉焉；少则洋洋焉，攸然而逝。子产曰：得其所哉！得其所哉！校人出，曰：孰谓子产智？予既烹而食之。曰：得其所哉！得其所哉！故君子可欺以其方，难罔以非其道。彼以爱兄之道来，故诚信而喜之，奚伪焉？

Book of Wan Zhang, Part I

Wan Zhang asked, "When Shun went into the fields, he cried out and wept to the pitying heavens. Why did he cry out and weep?" Mencius said, "Because he felt resentment and longing."
Wan Zhang said, "When one's parents love him, he is pleased and never forgets it; when they dislike him, though he may labor, he feels no resentment. But did Shun feel resentment?"
Mencius replied, "Chang Xi asked Gongming Gao, 'Regarding Shun's going to the fields, I have received your instructions; but about his crying and weeping to the pitying heavens and to his parents, I do not understand.' Gongming Gao answered, 'This is not what you can understand.' Gongming Gao thought that the heart of a filial son could not be so indifferent: 'I, to the utmost of my strength, cultivate the fields, and thereby discharge my duty as a son. What is there in me that my parents do not love me?' The Emperor caused his nine sons and two daughters, the various officers, oxen and sheep, storehouses and granaries, all to be prepared, to serve Shun amid the channeled fields. Of the scholars of the empire, many came to him. The Emperor designed that he should superintend the empire along with himself, and then to transfer it to him. But because he was not in the good graces of his parents, he was like a poor man who has nowhere to turn.
That the scholars of the empire were pleased with him, was what men desire, but it was not sufficient to remove his sorrow. Beauty, what men desire—he had for his wives the two daughters of the Emperor, but this was not sufficient to remove his sorrow. Riches, what men desire—the wealth of the whole empire was his, but this was not sufficient to remove his sorrow. Honors, what men desire—the dignity of the Imperial dignity was his, but this was not sufficient to remove his sorrow. The reason why the being the object of men's pleasure, beauty, riches, and honors could not remove his sorrow, was that it could be removed only by his being in the good graces of his parents.
In his childhood, he felt attachment to his parents. When he became conscious of beauty, he felt attachment to young and beautiful women. When he had a wife and children, he felt attachment to them. When he obtained office, he felt attachment to his sovereign. If he could not get the favor of his sovereign, he felt agitated in his heart. But a great man only feels attachment to his parents all his life. At fifty, Shun's attachment was as strong as in his childhood. I have seen this in the case of the great Shun."
Wan Zhang asked, "It is said in the Book of Poetry, 'How does one take a wife? He must first inform his parents.' If the saying be true, no one should have exemplified it more than Shun. Why did Shun marry without informing them?"
Mencius said, "If he had informed them, he would not have been able to marry. That male and female should dwell together is the greatest of human relations. If Shun had informed them, he would have made void this greatest of human relations, thereby incurring their resentment. Therefore, he did not inform them."
Wan Zhang said, "As to Shun's marrying without informing his parents, I have received your instructions. But why did the Emperor give him his daughters as wives without informing Shun's parents?"
Mencius said, "The Emperor also knew that if he informed them, he could not give him his daughters as wives."
Wan Zhang said, "His parents set Shun to repair a granary, and then removed the ladder, and Gu Sou set fire to it. They sent him to dig a well, and then, coming out, they covered it up. Xiang said, 'The scheme to cover up the city-forming prince was all my achievement. The oxen and sheep are for my parents; the storehouses and granaries are for my parents. The spears and shields are mine; the lute is mine; the bow is mine; and my two sisters I shall make attend to my bed.' Xiang then went into Shun's palace, and there was Shun on his couch playing the lute. Xiang said, 'I am come, thinking anxiously of you, my lord.' He was confused and ashamed. Shun said, 'All my ministers and people, you may manage them for me.' I do not know whether Shun was ignorant of Xiang's intention to kill him."
Mencius said, "How could he be ignorant of it? When Xiang was sorrowful, he was sorrowful; when Xiang was joyful, he was joyful."
Wan Zhang said, "Then was Shun's joy hypocritical?"
Mencius said, "No. Formerly, someone sent a present of a live fish to Zichan of Zheng. Zichan ordered his pond-keeper to keep it in the pond. But the pond-keeper cooked it, and reported back, saying, 'When I first let it go, it appeared embarrassed. In a little while, it seemed to be at ease, and then it swam away joyfully.' Zichan said, 'It has got into its element! It has got into its element!' The pond-keeper went out and said, 'Who says Zichan is wise? I had cooked and eaten the fish, and he said, 'It has got into its element! It has got into its element!'' Therefore, a superior man may be deceived by what seems to be reasonable, but he cannot be entrapped by what is contrary to principle. Xiang came in the way of a brother showing affection; therefore, Shun sincerely believed him and was joyful. How could that be hypocrisy?"

en:
[I]

Wang Rong was concise and essential, while Pei Kai was clear and penetrating.
Kongming was known as the Sleeping Dragon; Lu Wang was foretold as "not a bear."
Yang Zhen of Guanxi, Ding Kuan of Yidong.
Xie An, noble and pure; Wang Dao, loyal and just.
Kuang Heng bored a hole through the wall for light; Sun Jing locked himself indoors to study.
Zhi Du, the azure eagle; Ning Cheng, the nursing tiger.
Zhou Song was stubborn and unyielding; Liang Ji was arrogant and domineering.
Xi Chao's whiskered counsel, Wang Xun's brief memoranda.
Fubo's marker pillar, Bowang's quest for the river's source.
Li Ling's early verses, Tian Heng's mournful song.
Wuzhong wrote tirelessly; Shiheng worried about having too much talent.
Huan Tan denounced prophecy, Wang Shang dispelled rumors.
Ji and Lu summoned each other's carriages; Cheng and Kong tilted their canopies in friendship.
Ju Meng alone could match an army; Zhou Chu rid the land of the three plagues.
Hu Guang made up for the emperor's shortcomings; Yuan An became the pillar the state relied upon.
Huang Ba excelled in local administration; Liang Xi achieved the highest rank in regional governance.
Mozi wept over dyed silk; Yang Zhu wept at the forked road.
Zhu Bo's crows gathered, Xiao Zhi's pheasants followed.
Du Hou grew new teeth, King Ling of Zhou grew a beard.
Jia Yi feared the owl, Zhuangzi dreaded being a sacrificial ox.
King Zhao of Yan built the Golden Terrace; Zheng Zhuang established courier stations to welcome guests.
Guan and Jing, twin marvels of calligraphy; Yue and Zhan, paired jades of talent.
Qie Shen's single branch, Dai Feng's honored seat.
Zou Yang's long robe, Wang Fu's plain sleeves.
The crying crane beneath the sun, Shilong amid the clouds.
Emperor Xuan of Jin possessed the wary wolf-like gaze; Emperor Zu of Han bore the auspicious dragon-like countenance.
Bao Jing remembered the well, Yang Hu recognized the ring.
Zhong Rong, lofty as the blue clouds; Shuye, pure as Mount Yu.
Mao Yi received the summons with reverence, Zilu carried rice for his parents.
Jiang Ge, loyal and filial; Wang Lan, devoted to his brother.
Xiao He established the laws, Shusun crafted the rites.
Ge Feng exposed wrongdoing, Xi Gong endured constant slander.
Guan Ning cut the straw mat to sever a friendship; He Qiao occupied a whole carriage due to his obsession with money.
Shi Miao left his calf behind, Yang Xu hung up his fish.
Fan Kui pushed open the door, Xin Pi pulled at his robe.
Sun Chu "rinsed with stone," Hao Long "sunbathed his books."
Mei Gao petitioned the palace, Chong Guo praised his own service.
Wang Yan judged men by their air, Xu Shao rated them monthly.
He Xun, foremost of Confucian scholars; Sun Chuo, crowned in talent.
Taishu was eloquent and learned, Zhi Zhong skilled in letters.
Shan Tao had deep insight, Mao Jie was just and upright.
Yuan Ang refused his seat, Wei Guan struck the bed in sorrow.
Lord Yu's gate stood tall, Cao Can packed swiftly for duty.
A humble woman's plea stirred the wind, Zou Yan's grief brought frost.
Fan Dan let dust settle, Yan Ying ate coarse grain.
Jiefen rose to found Wei, Bieling ruled as king of Shu.
Buyi was falsely accused of theft, Bian He wept over his jade.
Tan Qing danced as a monkey, Xie Shang mimicked the myna.
Taichu shone like sun and moon, Jiye chronicled the seasons.
Xun and Chen, stars of virtue; Li and Guo, immortals on a boat.
Wang Tun's embroidered quilt, Lady Zhang's bronze hook.
Lord Ding was swiftly executed, Yong Chi was first enfeoffed.
Chen and Lei, bound like glue and lacquer; Fan and Zhang, sharing chicken and millet.
Marquis Zhou stood firm as a mountain, his fame rose like mist over Kuaiji.
Ji Bu's single promise, Ruan Zhan's three words.
Guo Wen roamed freely among mountains; Yuan Hong moored his boat by the river islet to compose poetry.
Huang Wan discoursed on the sun, Qin Mi debated the heavens.
Meng Ke cultivated simplicity; Yang Xiong composed the Xuan.
Xiang Xiu wept at the flute's sound, Bo Ya broke his strings.
Guo Huai humbled herself, and even Nan Commandery pitied her.
Lu Gong tamed the pheasants, Song Jun banished the beasts.
Yue Guang's guest was startled by a bow's reflection mistaken for a snake; Yin Hao observed the constellations to predict political shifts.
Yuanli set the standard, Jiyan led as its chief.
Lu Bao wrote the Satire on the God of Money; Cui Lie's reputation was tainted by the smell of copper cash.
Liang Song was honored with temple offerings, Zhao Wen soared like an eagle.
Mei Cheng rode the padded cart, Zheng Jun wore plain white robes.
Ling's mother fell upon her sword; Ke's mother cut the loom's thread.
The Qi consort broke the jade ring, Lady Xie resolved the siege.
Zaochi's letters, Xun Xu's musical harmony.
Hu Wei declined the silk; Lu Ji held onto the oranges.
Luo Han swallowed the bird in his dream, Jiang Yan dreamed of the writing brush.
Li Xin was pure and steadfast; Liu Lin was lofty and forthright.
Jiang Xu tended his three paths, Xu You carried but a single gourd.
Yang Pu moved the pass; Du Yu built the bridge.
Shou Wang debated the cauldron; Du Lin refuted claims about Yao.

zh:
“为人做事，需用真心。”史真的父母是这样为他解释他的名字的。
一门祖业，一颗诚心，这位江南的小伙子，也曾是街坊四邻有口皆碑的好商贩。
可惜，未央城看上了史真的生意。
普通人能挣的钱，未央城自然也能挣，而未央城若是能挣，便不会让给普通人挣。

失了生计，他只能一件件变卖家当，直到只剩下一身破烂的衣裳。他流落街头，与犬争食，几次与死亡擦肩而过，他顾不得曾经拥有过的体面了，他只想活，他从几十个人里，抢出了东阙公子掷出的玉玦，顾不得眼睛里流下的血挡住了视线，他把那玉玦举得极高，他知道那玉玦能让他东山再起，他不介意那是仇家的玉玦。甚至……他走进了未央城。
温无痕问他姓名的时候，他沉默了一会儿，说他叫史鸩。他觉得自己以前都活错了，什么真心都是狗屁，别人若是毒，他就比别人还毒，他要重新活，他要做那个在黄金马车上扔玉玦的人，他要别人都注视着他，如同注视着神明。
他做到了，他终于见到那高高在上的东阙公子像一块烂泥一样落入水里，可那温无痕竟还是看不起他。
王侯将相宁有种乎？凭什么你们温家代代为财神，他不服。

他窃了未央城的武学秘籍，找到了绣金楼的主人，拥有了两个新的身份。
绣金楼的玄林掌司，和开封府的判官。
这两个身份，足以使他成为天下的新财神。
en:
"To act in this world, one must do so with a true heart." This was how Shi Zhen's parents had explained the meaning of his name.
With a family business and an earnest heart, the young man from Jiangnan had once been a respected merchant, praised by neighbors for his integrity.
Until Weiyang City set its sights on his livelihood. If commoners could profit from a trade, so could Weiyang City, and if Weiyang City could profit, it would never leave crumbs for others.

Bankrupt, he sold off every possession until he wore nothing but rags. Reduced to scavenging for food with stray dogs, cheating death time and again, he abandoned all pride. He fought through a mob to seize the jade pendant tossed by the Ember of East, blood streaming from his eye as he held the pendant aloft. He knew it could revive his fortune. He didn't care that it belonged to his enemy. And... he even walked into Weiyang City.
When Wen Wuhen asked his name, he paused. "Shi Jiu," he said. He has lived a fool's life. Sincerity was worthless. If others were venomous, he would be deadlier. He would rise anew, become the one tossing jade pendants from a golden wagon and make others gaze at him like a god.
He succeeded. He watched the lofty Ember of East fall into the mud like rotten flesh. But even then, Wen Wuhen scorned him.
Are nobles born, or made? Why should the Wen family rule as the God of Wealth for generations? He refused to accept it.

He stole Weiyang City's martial arts secret manuals, bargained with the master of Aureate Pavilion, and assumed two new identities: 
Mystic Supervisor of Aureate Pavilion, and Magistrate of Kaifeng Prefecture.

招财是一只被烧瓷人收养的小猫。
那时，它被烧瓷师傅们建窑生火的动静所吸引，在附近探头探脑，被宋九的师傅一把抓住。
“弟兄们，瞧，柴王爷保佑咱们，派来狸奴恭贺呢！”
宋九不忿，“师傅，猫来穷，狗来富，来条狗才好呢！”
“瞎说，我看，这一定是只招财猫！”，宋九的师傅万分笃定。
很多年过去，宋九的师傅都没了，瓷窑也没能发了财。
一如当初宋九说的，招财或许真的不是一只招财猫。

就好像，那位师傅也还在瓷窑一样。
en:
Wealthcall was adopted by the kiln workers. 
She had been sneaking around the kiln, drawn by the noise of firing porcelain. She was caught by Song Jiu's master. 
"Brothers, look! The Chai King has blessed us and brought us fortune!" 
Song Jiu was unconvinced: "Master, cats bring poverty, dogs bring wealth. We should've gotten a dog!" 
"Nonsense. This is definitely a lucky cat!" the master declared. 
Years passed. The master was gone, the Porcelain Kiln never did bring riches. 
Perhaps Song Jiu was right—Wealthcall was never meant to be a lucky cat. 
But her name never changed, and she's still there. 
As if that old master were still at the Porcelain Kiln too.

zh: 后来，镇上办起了蒙学。先生不光教认字，还教《孙子兵法》《史记》里的打仗故事。那些半大娃娃学了史书，回头再下棋，路子野得很——什么“瞒天过海”“暗度陈仓”，把孟节的老套路杀得七零八落。连败三局之后，孟节终于认清了形势：不是自己变弱了，是这帮娃娃太狡猾。第二天一早，他就把棋摊搬到了镇口，离蒙学越远越好。路过的人问他怎么换地方了，孟节咳了一声：“这儿……风景好。”
en: Everything changed when the town opened its first primary school. The schoolmaster there didn't just teach the children how to read and write. He filled their heads with grand military campaigns from the Art of War and the Records of the Grand Historian. Armed with this tactical lore, a handful of these half-grown scholars soon wandered over to Meng Jie's chessboard. Their playstyle was wildly, ruthlessly unorthodox. Deploying classic wartime stratagems, feigning weakness, laying decoys, and launching hidden flank attacks, they took the Chess King's tired, predictable routines and tore them to absolute shreds. After suffering three humiliating defeats in a row, Meng Jie was forced to face a bitter truth: it wasn't that his own skills had dulled. It was that these little brats had become far too cunning. Bright and early the very next morning, Meng Jie packed up his board and hauled his stall to the dusty outskirts of town, putting as much physical distance between himself and the Primary Academy as humanly possible. When a passing neighbor asked why on earth he had abandoned his prime spot at the crossroads, Meng Jie refused to meet his eye. He just gave a stiff, awkward cough. "The scenery out here... It's just much nicer."

zh: 孟节年轻时，是个不服输的主。那一年，他揣着棋盘从街头杀到巷尾，连挑十一名街坊，杀得镇上再无人敢应战。从此，“涌泉镇棋王”的名号便落到了他头上。孟节得意了十几年，逢人便说：“下棋这事儿，靠的是天赋，你们学不来的。”他把棋摊摆在镇中最热闹的十字街，每日泡一壶茶，等对手上门。可惜，一个能打的都没有。
en: In his younger days, Meng Jie was a man who simply refused to lose. One year, he tucked his chessboard under his arm and marched from one end of town to the other, laying waste to the local competition. He dismantled eleven neighbors in a row, playing until there wasn't a single soul left in Wellspring Town who dared pull up a chair opposite him. Overnight, he was crowned the undisputed "Chess King of Wellspring Town." Meng Jie happily coasted on that glory for well over a decade. "The board requires a certain innate genius," he'd brag to anyone within earshot. "It's not something the rest of you can just learn." Every morning, he held court at the town's busiest intersection, brewing a fresh pot of tea and waiting for a worthy challenger. Alas, no one was ever worth their salt.

想到这里，史鸩拿起了自己的金蟾弓。那一日，未央城大量财宝失窃，其中最为值钱的，是未央城的独门武学秘籍。

"A God of Wealth remains a god, even in the mud. But a toad... No matter how gilded, is still just a beast." 
The Ember of East's fall and Wen Wuhen's rise to power owed much to Shi Zhen's cunning. He had expected a reward worthy of his deeds, only to be met with scorn from the Wen family. 
Birthright? Nonsense. In this world, wealth is what makes a god. Whether you're born with a golden spoon or not is not important, after all... It can always be stolen. 
With that thought, Shi Zhen picked up his Golden Toad Bow.
That day, a fortune vanished from Weiyang City. The most priceless of all was a martial arts manual known only to its masters. 
Shi Zhen offered it as his pledge of loyalty to the mistress of Aureate Pavilion. 
"What a coincidence, you're a Shi too. There's a role in Kaifeng that suits you perfectly," the mistress said with a smile.

本人以村口大树下那只活了八年的大公鸡的性命发誓，文中所载，字字皆真。
                                                                             今行
武今行，开封之杰士也。才高八斗，为城中贵女所悦。然行志在寻访天下学问之广博，是以心不系于儿女情长。
值花朝之期，行遇一女子，为恶徒所困。行见义勇为，奋然援手，女得以脱险。及归，女邀其入室共品香茗，行以礼自持，婉拒之。自此，二人缘定，频见于开封街巷之间。或雨日同舟煮茗，或雪夜对弈围炉，又或春日共赏纸鸢高飞。两心渐近，相约于花灯璀璨之下。然行深思，求道之人，当以学问为先，情爱之事，恐绊足于前，故至暮不去。岁月流转，再逢此女，已跃居樊楼之巅。
行回首往昔，心有怅然，遂执笔以记之，以志其憾也。
en:
Let it be sworn upon the eight-year-old rooster at the village tree: every word here is true.
Jinhang
Wu Jinhang was Kaifeng's most celebrated scholar, a man whose brilliance lit poetry contests and philosophical debates alike. Noble daughters sighed over his verses, but Jinhang remained indifferent to courtship. Academia, not affection, ruled his heart.
Everything changed at the Flower Festival. When he rescued a silk-clad woman from drunken assailants, she offered tea in gratitude. Ever proper, he declined with a courteous bow. Yet fate entwined them: mornings found them meeting along lanes by chance; evenings dissolved into chess matches by winter hearths; spring afternoons spent chasing paper kites through peach-blossom gusts. Slowly, inexorably, the two were drawn close, and they agreed to meet by the lanterns. Yet a seeker of truth must walk the path unencumbered, he told himself. Love would only weigh his steps. So when dusk deepened, he turned homeward alone. Years later, he saw her again, perched atop Fan Tower like a phoenix alighting upon the Revelry Hall.
With bittersweet remembrance, he recorded this account. Some regrets never fade.

zh:
冯夷从未想过，自己有朝一日会成为“河伯”。年少支着咸鱼摊儿叫卖时没有，目见契丹入寇时没有，路遇洪水滔天时也没有。不是所有人都要做话本的主角，不论是济世的英雄，还是虚妄的神祇——因为不值。人不是为了别人活，天地逍遥，来去孑然。人，总是为了自己。
所以冯夷不懂她，不懂这天下第一自找麻烦之人，不懂张氏托孤之时，她为何要戴上河伯的面具。明明自是凡人一个，为何要贴金涂泥，去做泥塑的菩萨。
“阿鱼，值得么？”冯夷终于还是问出了口。
那人却只是笑笑，望着波光粼粼的黄河。
“或许有一天，不值得也会变成值得。”
这一天或许以另一种方式到来了。漫天的冷雨、滔天的洪水、紧闭的城门，和……倒在了冯夷怀里，再也没有生气的那个人。
“阿鱼，不值得……这世道，不值得。”
en:
Feng Yi never thought he would one day become the River Master. Not when he hawked dried fish as a boy. Not when he saw the Khitan invade. Not even when the floodwaters rose high enough to drown the sky; Not everyone is born to be the hero of a storybook. He is not the kind who saves the world, and certainly not some imagined god. Because it isn't worth it. People aren't born to live for others. Roaming in this vast and indifferent world, in the end, we all come and go alone. We live, always, for ourselves.
That's why Feng Yi never understands her. Never understands the one in the world most skilled at getting herself into trouble. Never understands why, when the Zhang family entrusted her with a child, she chose to wear the River Master's mask. She is just a mortal. So why pretend to be an immortal? Why gild herself in myth, coat herself in mud, and become a clay idol for others to worship?"
A Yu... was it worth it?" Feng Yi finally asked.
She only smiled, eyes fixed on the shimmering currents of the Yellow River.
"Maybe," she said, "one day, what isn't worth it... will be."
And perhaps that day does come in the form of freezing rain from a colorless sky, of floodwaters surging higher than walls can hold, of city gates that will not open, and of her, collapsing lifeless into Feng Yi's arms.
"Ah Yu," he whispered, "It wasn't worth it. This world... it's not worth it."

听说河东有村叫王富的员外年近六十，新纳一十八岁的妾。不料半月后，小妾与账房先生卷了金银跑了。王员外气瘫了。
听山阳城孙家老婆子说他主家的四郎，腿被打断了。其他几个兄弟商量着把他赶出去。
听一书生说他去某某客栈投宿，半夜偷看隔壁，见一光头和尚搂着妇人。次日告与店家，店家笑说是东家娘子，素来信佛，请高僧来讲经的。
听卖柴火的刘三说城西豆腐坊赵寡妇，皮肤白嫩，人称豆腐西施。绸缎庄孙家四郎，天天去买豆腐，一进后厨就是半个时辰。
听说春香楼老鸨周某，近日被人半夜用锐器戳中心口，人当场死了，本来她就经常克扣手下妓女的赎身钱，这下都没人给她下葬。
听说某某地有三人都亲耳听到李财主家的骡子，忽然开口说了句人话，自言“今年收成不好”。请道士来做法，道士说骡子活不过三日。果然第三天骡子倒地死了。
听说北边道上出了个怪人，专抢过路商贩的鞋子。不抢银子不抢货，只把两只鞋子扒走，留下光脚。有个被抢的商人骂了句晦气，第二天就摔断了腿。有人说是山精作怪，也有人说是个疯乞丐。
听说曲城南王阿婆卖菜，少给了客几两，被人发现之后，王阿婆当街谩骂起来，正巧一姓澹台的捕快路过撞见。捕快说“欺诈骗秤，又口出恶言”，当场就要剪了那王阿婆的舌头。众人跪了一地求情，最后判她自扇五十个耳光，王阿婆吓得半个月没敢出门。
近日在客栈歇脚，一对男女眉来眼去，分明是勾搭上了。路人上前搭话，那两人竟不理。呵，路人一看便知，那女子不是良家，那男子迷了心窍。路人义愤填膺，便先去诈那女子，暗示她的底细已被那男子全抖给了别人，那男子不过是骗她的；转脸又去劝那男子，说那女子专是做仙人跳的，男子怕是要被骗个人财两空。顺便把什么春香楼的“老家”讲了讲清楚。不到半日，那对男女必然得分开，路人也算是救人前程。这路人是谁呢？那必然是好心的我了。
en:
Found in: Room Earth II Right

In business, nothing matters more than sharp eyes and keen ears. These are notes gathered from my travels, sure to prove useful someday!

I heard that Squire Wang Fu of a village in Hedong, nearly sixty years old, recently took an eighteen-year-old concubine. Half a month later, she ran off with the accountant and all his gold and silver, leaving Squire Wang bedridden with rage.
Old Matriarch Sun of Shanyang City said the fourth son of her master's household had his leg broken, and his brothers are plotting to cast him out.
A scholar claimed that while lodging at an inn, he peeked into the next room at midnight and saw a bald monk embracing a woman. When he reported it the next morning, the innkeeper laughed and explained it was the mistress of the house, a devout Buddhist who had invited the monk to explain the sutras.
Liu San the woodcutter said Widow Zhao at the West City Tofu Shop has skin so fair she is called the Tofu Belle. The fourth son of the Sun Silk Shop visits her shop daily, lingering in the kitchen for half an hour each time.
I heard Madam Zhou of Fragrance Pavilion was stabbed through the heart at midnight and died instantly. Having constantly skimmed the redemption funds of her courtesans, she now has no one willing to bury her.
Three people in a nearby town swore they heard Landlord Li's mule speak in human tongue, muttering, "The harvest will be poor this year." A Daoist priest was hired to perform a ritual and predicted the beast would not live three days. Sure enough, it dropped dead on the third day.
Word is that a bizarre rogue appeared on the northern road, robbing passing merchants of nothing but their shoes. Leaving them barefoot without taking a single coin or scrap of cargo. One merchant cursed his luck and broke his leg the very next day. Some claim it is a mountain spirit at work, while others say it is just a mad beggar.
Granny Wang in southern Qucheng was caught shortchanging vegetable weights and hurled vile curses in the street, only to run into a constable surnamed Tantai. Declaring her guilty of "deceitful weights and foul speech," the constable moved to slit her tongue on the spot. The crowd knelt to plead for her, and she was ultimately sentenced to slap herself fifty times, leaving her too terrified to step outside for half a month.
Recently, while resting at an inn, a bystander noticed a man and woman exchanging flirtatious glances, clearly up to no good. The same bystander approached to chat, but they ignored him. Hah! One glance told the bystander that the woman was no respectable lady, and the man was utterly bewitched. Righteous indignation stirred within him: he first deceived the woman, hinting that the man had already spilled her past to others and was merely using her; then he turned to warn the man that she was running a badger game and would leave him penniless, making sure to lay bare the truth about Fragrance Pavilion. In less than half a day, the pair had parted ways, their futures saved by that bystander.
And who was that bystander? Why, kindhearted me, of course.

在中国传统文化中，雾与豹似乎有着天然的亲缘关系。其一，因豹善隐雾中，其二，雾与豹经常在隐逸诗中联袂出现。雾豹原型可追溯到刘向《列女传》关于陶荅子妻故事中“南山有玄豹，雾雨七日不下食”的记载，但雾豹的使用却是中唐以后的事。多用来比喻隐逸山林的隐士之事。
en:
A tiger that knows better stays in its cage; a leopard content hides in the mist.

In traditional Chinese culture, mist and leopards share a natural bond. One, because leopards hide well in mist; two, because they often appear together in hermit poetry. The prototype traces back to Liu Xiang's Biographies of Exemplary Women, where a black leopard stays in the mountains for seven days without eating during rain and mist. It is often a metaphor for scholars living in seclusion.
